sections.heading: AA against AI, compared through the degree the student actually wants
paragraphs: Comparing the two courses on content alone produces a stalemate, because each is harder than the other somewhere. The useful comparison runs backwards from the degree. Certain routes commonly specify Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level, sometimes with a minimum grade. Others accept either course. A few are indifferent to mathematics entirely, and a student in that position who takes AA HL out of caution has bought two difficult years for nothing.

The rule for checking is strict and worth following. Read the entry requirements on the university's own admissions page, for the intake year the student will apply to, for the named programme. Requirements vary between institutions and change between years. No tutoring page, including this one, should be treated as the source for a requirement that determines a two-year course choice, and any site presenting a blanket list of degree-to-course mappings is simplifying something that varies.

What can be said generally is the pattern of fit. Engineering, mathematics, physics and many economics routes commonly expect the algebraic and calculus-heavy content that AA provides, and a student arriving at such a degree from AI can find the first year steeper. Business, design, psychology and several health-science routes commonly accept AI, and for a student who thinks statistically the AI course is a better two years and often a better grade.

The student's own disposition is the tiebreaker and it is legitimate evidence rather than sentiment. A student who enjoys exactness and proof will work harder in AA and do better. A student who wants to know what a number means in context will engage with AI and produce a stronger Exploration. Two years is long enough that enjoyment compounds into grades, which is why pushing a statistically minded student into AA for prestige tends to produce neither the grade nor the interest.

sections.heading: Diploma mathematics against A-Level mathematics, as two post-16 routes
paragraphs: Several Abu Dhabi schools run a British curriculum to Year 11 and then offer either A-Levels or the Diploma, which makes this a live comparison for Al Rawdah families rather than an abstract one. The two routes produce different workloads, different kinds of mathematics and different university conversations, and the comparison is rarely made properly before the decision is taken.

A-Level mathematics is narrower and deeper. Three or four subjects, pure mathematics with mechanics or statistics, no coursework, no core, and the student's whole timetable pointing at a small number of papers. A student who already knows they want engineering and dislikes essay subjects often thrives here. The Diploma is broader: six subjects, three at Higher Level, Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay, and a 20% Exploration inside mathematics itself.

For tutoring the practical difference is where the pressure lands. An A-Level student needs sustained technical work across two years with the pressure concentrated in the examination series. A Diploma student needs the same technical work plus management of internal deadlines that arrive throughout, which is why Diploma tutoring is more often seasonal and deadline-shaped while A-Level tutoring is more often steady.

On equivalency the routes are documented differently. For the British track, the Ministry of Education's requirements are published: one accredited subject at Advanced Level at no less than grade E or two at Advanced Subsidiary Level at the same grade, plus five accredited GCSE or IGCSE subjects at no less than E or grade 3, with Arabic and Islamic education excluded from that five. No IB points threshold appears in that source, so a family should verify the IB position on moe.gov.ae rather than accept a figure from a commercial page.

sections.heading: The step from IGCSE into Diploma maths, and what it actually costs to close
paragraphs: Most Al Rawdah Diploma students arrive from IGCSE, and the transition has a predictable shape. An Extended or Higher-tier IGCSE student has strong algebra, confident trigonometry, reasonable statistics and essentially no calculus. The first term of DP1 introduces calculus quickly and assumes an algebraic fluency that IGCSE rewarded but did not require under sustained time pressure.

The gap is narrow and specific, which is good news. Surds and index laws at speed, standard form, the factor and remainder theorems, function notation used precisely, and the habit of writing a solution a marker can follow without guessing. Eight to twelve sessions in DP1 term one normally closes it. The same gap discovered in DP2 costs considerably more, because by then it sits under a year of newer content that also needs attention.

Students arriving from the Middle Years Programme have a different gap: investigation skills are strong, formal proof and timed technical writing are not. Students arriving from CBSE often have more calculus than the course needs and no experience of a graphical display calculator. Each of these is a different eight-week plan, and a tutor who offers the same plan to all three has not asked where the student came from.

The comparison worth making here is about timing rather than tutor. Buying help in September is cheaper than buying it in February for exactly the same problem, because in September the problem is one topic and in February it is one topic plus everything built on top of it. Families routinely wait for a report card to justify the spend, which is understandable and expensive.

sections.heading: Comparing formats by what a monthly budget actually buys
paragraphs: Set a monthly figure and see what each format delivers for it, which is a more honest comparison than an hourly rate. Bestimate's 2026 estimates for weekly one-hour sessions put budget tuition at AED 240 to 600 a month, mid-range at AED 600 to 1,200, and specialist exam-year work at AED 1,000 to 2,000 or more. Advertised monthly packages in this market include AED 799 for eight online sessions and AED 1,599 to 1,799 for four two-hour in-home sessions.

Read those two packages against each other. Eight online sessions a month at AED 799 is roughly twice the contact of four in-home sessions at AED 1,599 to 1,799, for less than half the money. The in-home figure is not a rip-off; it is what the format costs once travel is inside it. But a family deciding between them should see that the comparison is eight hours against eight hours at very different prices, or eight hours against four at double the cost.

The hourly bands behind all of this, read in October 2026: budget online AED 45 to 150, with EdFlik publishing AED 45 to 65 and Tutopiya from AED 33 to 52; qualified online subject tutor AED 150 to 300, with Unitors publishing IB from AED 200; in-home AED 180 to 500 with travel included, Bestimate quoting AED 180 to 350; specialists AED 200 to 450 and upwards, TutorChase publishing AED 270; premium examiner-led AED 500 to 650 and above, BartyED publishing AED 650.

For context, the comparison families most often make is against school fees rather than against other tutors. KHDA confirmed on 22 May 2026 that there would be no increase in private school fees in Dubai for the 2026-27 academic year, under an incentives package valued at AED 1.5 billion within a AED 2.5 billion total; Abu Dhabi fees are regulated separately by ADEK. Every tutoring figure quoted here is a market rate from a named published source, not an IB Gram price; ours comes after the free trial lesson.

sections.heading: The pool comparison, and what we do when the right tutor is not free
paragraphs: The final comparison is the one that justifies the format. An in-home arrangement selects from adults who will travel to Al Rawdah at the hour you need. An online arrangement selects from adults who have taught your child's course at their level. For AA Standard Level those sets overlap reasonably. For AA Higher Level Paper 3, or AI Higher Level statistics, they frequently do not overlap at all in a market the size of Abu Dhabi.

Being honest about that cuts both ways, because it means our own pool is finite too. Higher Level mathematics specialists fill up, particularly in the weeks before mock windows and internal assessment deadlines. When nobody is free for a course, you are told, given an expected wait, and offered the alternatives in writing rather than quietly matched to whoever is available.

Those alternatives are specific: another qualified tutor on the same course in a different slot; a tutor based outside the UAE teaching the same IB course on Gulf Standard Time, disclosed before you book rather than after; shorter and more frequent sessions until the preferred slot clears; or a named wait. In DP1 term one, waiting is often the right answer rather than a disappointment, because nothing is yet urgent.

The free trial lesson is where all of these comparisons stop being abstract. One full lesson with the matched tutor, no card required, used to establish whether the course and level are right, where the marks are going, whether the Exploration is on track, and whether these two people work well together. If the match is wrong we change it. If the honest finding is that your child needs three sessions rather than thirty, that is what you should hear.

process.title: Tell us the course, the level and the target
process.description: AA or AI, Higher or Standard, the school, and what the student is aiming at after school. The last part matters because it determines whether the current level is the right one, which is a bigger question than any topic gap.

process.title: We check the comparison before selling hours
process.description: If the course or level looks wrong on the evidence, you hear that first. A short advisory session works sample questions from both courses and reports what happened, and the summary is written so you can take it to the school.

process.description: An AA Higher Level student is matched to a tutor who teaches AA Higher Level and can talk through a Paper 3 question. Where the specialist is not free, you get the wait and the alternatives rather than a near-enough substitute.

process.title: Free trial lesson, then a plan with an order
process.description: One full lesson, no card required. The tutor locates the real gap, checks the Exploration position, and builds a plan that spends time in proportion to marks rather than in syllabus order.

process.description: Every six to eight weeks the error log is compared with where it started. When the recurring failures have gone, the recommendation is fewer sessions or none. Renewal by default is how tutoring budgets quietly double.

whyPoints.description: A 7 at Standard Level usually serves a student better than a 4 at Higher Level, and we will say so. A provider whose first instinct is to encourage the higher level is selling hours rather than advising on a 45-point total.

whyPoints.title: Course fit checked against the real requirement
whyPoints.description: AA and AI diverge within a term. We check the named university's own admissions page for the intake year rather than repeating a generic mapping, because requirements vary between institutions and change between years.

whyPoints.title: Matched by course, not by distance
whyPoints.description: The adults who will drive to Al Rawdah are not the adults who have taught AA Higher Level. Online delivery makes course experience the selection criterion, which is the variable that actually moves a Paper 3 mark.

whyPoints.description: Eight online sessions advertised at AED 799 a month against four in-home sessions at AED 1,599 to 1,799 is the comparison families need, and it comes with its sources. Our own fee follows the free trial lesson.

whyPoints.description: A tutor narrows a question, teaches a technique and gives criterion-level feedback on the student's own draft. Nothing is written or calculated for the student, and no provider should offer to produce assessed work.

whyPoints.description: Higher Level specialists fill up before mock windows. You are told the wait in writing, and where a tutor is based outside the UAE you hear it before booking rather than after the first invoice.

faqs.question: Is Higher Level maths worth taking if the university will accept Standard Level?
faqs.answer: Usually not. A 7 at Standard Level protects the 45-point total and frees hours for the subjects the offer genuinely depends on, while a 4 at Higher Level helps nobody. Higher Level adds a third paper worth 20% of the grade and a body of content the Standard student never meets. The exceptions are real: engineering, mathematics, physics and many economics routes commonly expect Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level, so check the named programme's own admissions page for the intake year being applied to.

faqs.question: How early does the AA and AI decision become irreversible?
faqs.answer: In practice by the end of DP1 term one, and formally a little later depending on the school. The courses diverge quickly: an AA student meets implicit differentiation and complex numbers while an AI student meets chi-squared testing and the Poisson distribution, and those paths cannot be merged afterwards. That is why a single advisory conversation in Year 11, with sample questions from both courses worked in front of the student, is worth more than remedial tutoring in DP2.

faqs.question: Which Diploma maths course suits a student who likes statistics?
faqs.answer: Applications and Interpretation, in most cases, and it is worth saying that AI is genuinely harder than AA in the statistics strand rather than a lighter version of it. AI Higher Level reaches chi-squared testing, the Poisson distribution and hypothesis testing, which AA never covers. A statistically minded student pushed into AA for prestige tends to produce neither the grade nor the interest, and two years is long enough that engagement compounds into marks.

faqs.question: What does Paper 3 add that Standard Level students never see?
faqs.answer: Two extended problem-solving questions worth 20% of the Higher Level grade, running across syllabus topics and building from an accessible opening into unfamiliar territory. It rewards stamina and tidy notation rather than recall, and it cannot be prepared for by completing more short questions faster. This single component is the strongest practical reason to match a tutor to the exact level rather than to the subject, because a Standard Level specialist has never taught it.

faqs.question: We are choosing between the Diploma and A-Levels. How does maths compare?
faqs.answer: A-Level mathematics is narrower and deeper: three or four subjects, pure maths with mechanics or statistics, no coursework and pressure concentrated in the examination series. Diploma mathematics sits inside six subjects plus the core, carries a 20% Exploration, and spreads pressure across internal deadlines all year. A student certain about engineering who dislikes essay subjects often does better on A-Levels; a student who wants breadth or is undecided often does better on the Diploma.

faqs.question: How big is the jump from IGCSE maths into DP1?
faqs.answer: Narrow but steep. An Extended or Higher-tier IGCSE student arrives with strong algebra and trigonometry and essentially no calculus, and DP1 introduces calculus quickly while assuming algebraic fluency at speed. The specific gaps are surds and index laws under time pressure, standard form, the factor and remainder theorems, and writing a solution a marker can follow. Eight to twelve sessions in term one normally closes it; the same gap found in DP2 costs considerably more.

faqs.question: Why is buying help in September cheaper than buying it in February?
faqs.answer: Because in September the problem is one topic and in February it is one topic plus everything built on top of it. A calculus gap identified in term one takes a handful of sessions. The same gap discovered in a January mock has to be fixed alongside the newer content that also needs attention, which doubles the work and compresses it into less time. Families understandably wait for a report card to justify the spend, and that delay is the most expensive habit in Diploma tutoring.

faqs.question: Does an Al Rawdah family pay more for maths tuition than one in Al Mushrif?
faqs.answer: For online tuition there is no reason for any difference, and if a quote moves between two central addresses, what moved is travel. In-home rates do vary by distance, with published bands of AED 180 to 500 an hour including the journey, Bestimate quoting AED 180 to 350. A tutor who can chain two visits in a school-dense district sometimes quotes slightly less. None of this affects the course, the papers or the Exploration.

faqs.question: How does a monthly package compare between online and in-home tuition?
faqs.answer: Advertised packages in this market include AED 799 a month for eight online sessions and AED 1,599 to 1,799 a month for four two-hour in-home sessions. That is eight hours of contact against eight hours, at less than half the price, or eight sessions against four depending on how you count. The in-home figure is not unreasonable; it is what the format costs once travel sits inside it. Seeing both numbers together is what lets a family decide deliberately.

faqs.question: Can a tutor tell us whether our child is on the wrong course?
faqs.answer: A good one will, and it is uncomfortable rather than routine, which is why some providers avoid it. The evidence comes from working sample questions from both courses and both levels with the student and watching fluency, stamina and the response to an unfamiliar problem. A written summary of that session is something a family can take to the school. A first session that reports a wrong course is worth more than a term of competent teaching in the wrong one.

faqs.question: What does an AA Higher Level tutor do that a general maths tutor cannot?
faqs.answer: Teach proof by induction properly, work complex numbers in both Cartesian and polar form, handle implicit differentiation and differential equations, and prepare a student for Paper 3 by working whole extended questions untimed and then timed. A general maths tutor can usually support Standard Level content competently. The Higher Level extension is a different kind of mathematics rather than more of the same, and it shows within two or three sessions.

faqs.question: How is the Exploration marked, and what can a tutor legitimately do?
faqs.answer: It is marked out of 20 across five criteria, with use of mathematics carrying the most marks and presentation, communication, personal engagement and reflection carrying the rest. That means more than half the marks sit outside mathematical difficulty. A tutor can narrow the question, check the mathematics sits at course level, teach a technique the student applies, and give criterion-level feedback on a draft the student wrote. A tutor cannot write, calculate or edit any part of it to completion.

faqs.question: Are IB maths tutors in Abu Dhabi required to hold a permit?
faqs.answer: Individuals providing private tuition in the UAE need the MoHRE private tutor work permit, introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023 and granted free of charge for two years. Eligible applicants include registered school teachers, government and private-sector employees, unemployed residents, university students and school students aged 15 to 18. Those tutoring without one are subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws. No fine schedule is published, so distrust any amount quoted at you.

faqs.question: What if the AI Higher Level specialist we need is booked out?
faqs.answer: You are told, with an expected wait and the alternatives written down: another qualified tutor on the same course at a different time, a tutor based outside the UAE teaching the same course on Gulf Standard Time and disclosed before booking, shorter and more frequent sessions until the preferred slot clears, or a named wait. AI Higher Level is the narrowest specialism of the four combinations, and availability is tightest in the weeks before mock windows and Exploration deadlines.

abu-dhabi/ib-maths-tutor-in-al-rawdah.closingHeading: Settle the course question, then book the hours
abu-dhabi/ib-maths-tutor-in-al-rawdah.closingBody: Before paying for an IB maths tutor in Al Rawdah, it is worth knowing whether the course and the level are the right ones, because that decision outweighs the choice of tutor. Tell us the course, the level, the school and what your child is aiming at afterwards, and we will match a Diploma mathematics specialist and say plainly what the evidence shows, including when the honest answer is to change course rather than to buy lessons. The first lesson is free. Tuition runs one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time; home visits are a service we offer only in India.

abu-dhabi/ib-maths-tutor-in-al-reef.tutorsIntro: The tutors below teach Diploma Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches and Applications and Interpretation at both levels, for families in Al Reef and the airport-road corridor. Every match states the course and the level first, because the four courses share a name and little else.

intro.heading: What one weekly hour of IB mathematics can and cannot do
paragraphs: Al Reef households arrive at the same constraint as almost everybody out this way. The bus is long, the Diploma week already holds six subjects plus Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and CAS, and when the sums are done there is one reliable hour a week available for mathematics. Occasionally two. The useful planning question is therefore not how much tutoring to buy but what belongs inside that hour and what belongs outside it.

The distinction is real and it is the single most useful idea on this page. Some mathematics improves through explanation: a concept that has not landed, a technique nobody has demonstrated, a question type the student does not recognise. That work needs a teacher and fits an hour. Other mathematics improves only through repetition: algebraic fluency, mental estimation, exact-value arithmetic, recall of identities. That work needs fifteen minutes a day and gains almost nothing from a weekly lesson, because a week is long enough for the gain to decay before the next session.

Families who do not separate the two spend the scarce hour on the wrong half. A tutor runs algebra practice for sixty minutes, which is pleasant and produces a measurable improvement that has vanished by the following Tuesday, while the concept that was actually blocking progress goes untouched for another week. The correct arrangement is the reverse: the hour explains and diagnoses, the student drills daily, and the tutor checks the error pattern in the drills rather than running them.

The second thing worth settling early is which of the four Diploma mathematics courses your child is on. Analysis and Approaches and Applications and Interpretation each run at Higher and Standard Level, and they diverge in content, in calculator access and in paper structure. Analysis and Approaches at Standard Level sits Paper 1 without a calculator, which makes exact-value fluency a genuine examination requirement rather than good practice. Every Applications and Interpretation paper permits the calculator, which moves the work elsewhere entirely.

What follows is a method for spending one hour well. It sorts mathematics tasks into those that fit an hour and those that do not, sets out a fifteen-minute daily drill plan, explains how to read a marked Diploma script, breaks the exploration into tasks small enough for a full week, and lays out what to do in the eight weeks after a mock result. IB Gram provides no home visits in Abu Dhabi; visiting tutors are a service offered only in India, and every session described here reaches a desk over live video. Nothing in the method below depends on hiring anybody either: a family that separates the hour from the drill and reads the marked script has already done the part most arrangements get wrong.

abu-dhabi/ib-maths-tutor-in-al-reef.programmesIntro: Three programmes matter here: the Diploma, the Middle Years Programme that precedes it at the continuum schools in this corridor, and the IGCSE route most students arrive from. Each produces a different relationship between the weekly hour and the daily drill.

programmes.name: IB Diploma Programme mathematics
programmes.description: One course from four, covering number and algebra, functions, geometry and trigonometry, statistics and probability, and calculus to different depths. Higher Level carries roughly 240 taught hours against 150 at Standard and adds a third paper. The exploration is common to all four courses at twenty per cent of the final grade, marked out of twenty against five criteria.
programmes.countryNote: The document that governs an Al Reef Diploma student's year is the school's written internal deadline calendar, not anything the board publishes. Ask the IB coordinator for it at the start of Year 12. No IB examination or results date appears on this page, because the IB's own site blocks automated verification and an unverified date acted on by a family is worse than none.

programmes.name: IB Middle Years Programme mathematics
programmes.description: Criterion-referenced, graded 1 to 8 against four criteria, with extended and standard streams in the upper years. Students arrive in the Diploma strong on investigation and reasoning and slow at routine manipulation, because the programme credits the quality of mathematical thinking more than speed and accuracy under pressure.
programmes.countryNote: For an Al Reef student this profile makes the daily drill more important than the weekly hour in the first Diploma term, because what is missing is fluency rather than understanding. Fifteen minutes a day of indices, surds and rearrangement closes more of that gap in a month than four tutoring sessions would.

programmes.name: IGCSE and International GCSE mathematics
programmes.description: Cambridge 0580 Extended or Pearson Edexcel 4MA1 Higher in this corridor, with Additional Mathematics 0606 available in some schools. Students arrive with secure procedure and no experience of open-ended mathematical writing, which makes the exploration the unfamiliar part rather than the content.
programmes.countryNote: Students who completed 0606 arrive with most of the Analysis and Approaches entry gap closed and generally need the hour for exploration work rather than for content. Students who sat Core tier and want Analysis and Approaches need an honest conversation in Year 11, because Applications and Interpretation at Standard Level is usually the realistic route.

abu-dhabi/ib-maths-tutor-in-al-reef.subjectsIntro: Mathematics tasks sorted by what they need rather than by topic heading, because that sorting is what makes a single weekly hour productive.

subjects.name: Concept explanation
subjects.description: A topic that has not landed despite class teaching: implicit differentiation, hypothesis testing, vector geometry. This is what an hour is for, because it needs somebody to demonstrate and then watch the student attempt it. Nothing else returns as much per paid minute.

subjects.name: Question-type recognition
subjects.description: Learning to see what a question is asking for before starting. Students who can do every technique still lose marks because they do not recognise which one a question invites. Taught in an hour, reinforced by drills afterwards.

subjects.name: Algebraic fluency
subjects.description: Indices, surds, rearrangement, algebraic fractions. Essential and badly suited to a weekly lesson: it needs fifteen minutes a day. The tutor's role is to check the error pattern rather than to run the practice.

subjects.name: Exact-value arithmetic
subjects.description: Surds, fractions and trigonometric exact values handled quickly and accurately. A genuine examination requirement for Analysis and Approaches candidates, and purely a repetition task, so it belongs entirely in daily drills.

subjects.name: Calculator discipline
subjects.levels: All AI papers; AA Papers 2 and 3
subjects.description: Writing the equation before the screen value, storing rather than retyping, rounding once at the end, checking angle mode. A short taught habit with a large and immediate effect on marks that are currently being withheld rather than missed.

subjects.name: The exploration
subjects.description: Twenty per cent of the grade, marked out of twenty across criteria A to E, with only six marks for the mathematics being right. Decomposable into short tasks, which is why it suits a crowded Al Reef week better than families expect.

subjects.name: Paper 3 investigation
subjects.description: Two long structured problems in one hour at Higher Level. The one task that genuinely does not fit a sixty-minute slot, because a single investigation takes longer than that to attempt and review, so it needs a double session.

subjects.name: Timing and question selection
subjects.description: Deciding in the first few seconds whether to start a question and when to abandon one. Trainable, under-taught, and the thing that most often separates two students with identical knowledge. Practised in the hour, rehearsed in timed drills.

subjects.name: Command terms and notation
subjects.description: The difference between show that, find, justify and hence, and the notation an examiner expects. A reading skill rather than a mathematical one, and one that responds to two or three focused sessions and then stays fixed.

subjects.name: Statistics and the GDC together
subjects.description: Regression, distributions and hypothesis testing where the calculator produces the output and the marks depend on justifying it. Half concept and half discipline, so it needs both the hour and the drill.

sections.heading: Sorting tasks: what fits an hour and what does not
paragraphs: This is the decision that makes a single weekly hour worth paying for. Mathematics tasks divide into those that need a teacher present and those that need repetition, and the division is sharp enough to write down. Tasks needing a teacher involve something the student cannot currently do and could not reach alone: a concept that has not landed, a technique nobody has demonstrated, a question type they do not recognise, a method whose weakness they cannot see. Those fit an hour exactly.

Tasks needing repetition involve something the student can already do, just not fast or reliably enough. Algebraic rearrangement. Surd and fraction arithmetic. Recall of trigonometric identities. Mental estimation. Spotting a sign error. Every one of those improves with fifteen minutes a day and barely at all with sixty minutes a week, because the gain depends on frequency rather than duration and a seven-day gap undoes most of it before the next session.

Put the wrong task in the hour and the whole arrangement underperforms without obviously failing, which is why it persists. A session spent on algebra drill feels productive, produces visible improvement inside the hour, and leaves the concept that was actually blocking progress untouched for another week. The fix is to agree the split in writing at the start: the hour explains and diagnoses, the student drills daily, and the tutor opens each session by reading the drill errors rather than by setting more of them.

sections.heading: A fifteen-minute daily drill that actually gets done
paragraphs: A drill plan only works if it is short enough to survive a bad day, specific enough to need no decisions, and checkable without a parent becoming a teacher. Fifteen minutes is the right length because it fits after dinner on an evening when the bus was late, and because a student who is asked for thirty will do nothing on four days out of five. The content should be fixed for a fortnight at a time so there is nothing to choose each evening.

The structure that holds is five minutes of pure arithmetic or algebra at speed, five minutes on one targeted weakness, and five minutes of a single past-paper question attempted under a timer. The first block builds fluency. The second closes the specific gap the tutor identified. The third keeps timing in the student's habits rather than appearing as a panic in the final term. Written on a card or a shared note, with the week's content listed, it needs no planning from anybody.

The tutor's job is not to run the drill but to read it. Collect the week's work, look at where the errors cluster, and change next fortnight's second block accordingly. That takes a few minutes at the start of the session and converts the drill from homework into diagnosis. For an Al Reef student with one hour a week, this is how five hours of practice a fortnight appear without buying five hours of tutoring, and it is the difference between a plan that moves a grade and one that merely occupies an evening.

sections.heading: Reading a marked Diploma mathematics script
paragraphs: A marked paper is the most informative document an Al Reef family holds, and it is usually filed rather than read. It does not just show a mark; it shows how the mark was lost, and the pattern identifies which of several unrelated problems you are dealing with. Fifteen minutes with the script before any hours are bought is the highest-return effort available, and it also tells you quickly whether a prospective tutor is reading it or glancing at it.

Three signatures are worth looking for specifically. Questions where the final answer is correct but marks were still withheld point to invisible method, which on a calculator paper is usually a student writing a screen value without the equation that produced it. Questions blank or abandoned halfway, particularly clustered towards the end, point to timing rather than content. Questions attempted correctly with arithmetic errors scattered through them point to fluency, which is the drill problem rather than a teaching problem.

A fourth and subtler signature is the question answered correctly in the wrong form: an exact value given as a decimal, an answer to three significant figures where the question wanted two, a final line that does not state what was asked for. Those are reading losses and they are cheap to fix. A tutor who can walk through a script and classify every loss into those four categories within a few minutes is reading the paper properly, and that is a reasonable thing to require before the first paid session.

sections.heading: The exploration, in tasks small enough for a full week
paragraphs: The exploration is worth twenty per cent of the mathematics grade in all four courses and is routinely postponed, because it looks like a project and an Al Reef Diploma student has no room for a project. Broken into tasks it is not a project. It is a sequence of short decisions and short pieces of work, most of which fit inside a thirty-minute evening or inside the weekly hour alongside something else.

The sequence begins with the only task that cannot be rushed: testing whether the topic can generate mathematics at the course level. That is one conversation, and getting it wrong caps criterion E permanently regardless of how good the writing becomes. After that come securing data or a mathematical context, performing one analysis technique at a time, drafting one section at a time, and addressing one criterion at a time. Each of those is a discrete task with a visible finish, which is what makes them survivable in a crowded term.

Criteria A to E carry four, four, three, three and six marks respectively, and only criterion E is about the mathematics being correct. That means fourteen of the twenty marks reward how the piece is organised, communicated, owned and interrogated, which is work that can be done in short bursts. A tutor's legitimate contribution is teaching what each criterion credits, questioning method until the student finds its weakness, and marking drafts against the descriptors. No part of the exploration may be written, drafted or edited to submission by anybody but the student, at any price.

sections.heading: The eight weeks after a mock result
paragraphs: Mock results are the one moment in the Diploma when a family has precise information and a defined window to act on it. Eight weeks is roughly what exists between a mock and the next assessment point, and it is enough to move specific marks if the plan is built from the script rather than from anxiety. It is not enough to re-teach a course, and attempts to do that are why some families finish the period having covered everything and improved nothing.

The first fortnight belongs to the largest recoverable cluster from the script, which is usually either a single concept blocking several question types or the invisible-method habit on calculator papers. The second fortnight adds a full timed paper between sessions, marked against the scheme, so the pattern of losses can be compared with the original mock. By week five the comparison either shows movement in the targeted area or it does not, and that is the point to change the plan rather than extend it.

The last three weeks shift entirely to timing, question selection and finishing. Full papers under proper conditions, with the student practising the first-few-seconds decision about whether to start a question and the discipline of returning to an abandoned one. Nothing new is introduced after week six, because a topic met for the first time in the final fortnight is a liability rather than an asset. For an Al Reef household the whole block should be scheduled around the bus from the outset, because a plan that depends on three punctual weeks will not survive.

sections.heading: Which course, and why it changes the drill
paragraphs: The four Diploma mathematics courses do not simply differ in difficulty; they differ in what deserves daily practice. For Analysis and Approaches at either level, Paper 1 is sat without a calculator, which makes exact-value arithmetic, surd handling and fraction fluency genuine examination requirements. A student on that course who drills nothing daily will meet Paper 1 able to do every technique slowly, and slowness in a calculator-free paper is indistinguishable from not knowing.

For Applications and Interpretation, every paper permits the calculator, so the daily work moves to a different place: reading statistical output critically, recognising which model a context invites, and the discipline of justifying a screen value in writing. Higher Level adds matrices and graph theory, which are concept-heavy and belong in the paid hour rather than in drills, because they need demonstration before practice means anything.

The practical consequence is that a drill plan copied from another student is usually wrong. Ask any tutor to specify the daily drill for your child's specific course and level, and to say why that content rather than something else. Somebody teaching the course answers immediately and differently for Analysis and Approaches than for Applications and Interpretation. Somebody working from a general idea of Diploma mathematics will produce the same algebra sheet either way, which is the clearest available signal that the plan has not been built for your child. The same test works on an existing arrangement: ask what the drill is for and why, and listen for whether the answer names the course.

sections.heading: Honesty, permits and the two questions worth asking
paragraphs: Two short matters, both worth settling before money changes hands. The first is the exploration boundary. No tutor may write, draft, rewrite or edit to submission any part of an exploration, an Extended Essay, a Theory of Knowledge essay or any assessed coursework, at any price and under any deadline. It is submitted as the student's own work with a declaration, schools in this corridor run originality checks as routine, and a malpractice finding falls on the candidate rather than on whoever supplied the text. At least one provider in UAE search results sells completed Internal Assessments.

The second is the permit. Private tutoring in the UAE operates under Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, which introduced the MoHRE private tuition work permit, granted free of charge for two years. Eligible applicants include school teachers, government and private sector employees, unemployed residents, university students and students aged fifteen to eighteen. Tutoring without one brings fines and penalties under the applicable laws, and no fine schedule is published so no figure appears here.

There is a related Abu Dhabi rule. ADEK's professional-ethics requirements for private and charter school staff prohibit teachers from paid private tutoring of students enrolled at their own school, and the permit's code of conduct also bars serving students affiliated with the teacher's own school. That is press-reported rather than quoted from the policy document, so verify it against the current ADEK text. IB Gram holds no approval, accreditation or licence from ADEK, KHDA, the IB, Cambridge or Pearson, and any provider claiming otherwise is making a claim worth testing.

sections.heading: Testing a match in one free hour
paragraphs: Before any payment, one free hour over live video with no card details and no commitment. What makes it useful is deciding in advance what is being tested, because an unstructured trial becomes an introduction and leaves you deciding on exactly the impressions you were trying to get past.

Send the course and level, the school, a marked script and, if there is an exploration under way, its current state. Then watch three things in the hour. Does the tutor work from that material rather than from a generic topic? Can they classify every loss on the script into method, timing, fluency or reading? And do they specify a daily drill for your child's course and level, with a reason for that content rather than another?

Afterwards ask your child a single question: did you follow it? That is the judgement nobody else can make and the one that predicts whether the arrangement will work, because a student who will not interrupt to ask something is paying for a monologue. Then ask the provider the two closing questions: what happens if the match is wrong, and what will you refuse to do. Three providers tested the same way inside a week gives a real comparison, which is quicker and cheaper than arranging for anybody to drive to Al Reef. Keep the written answers as well, because a provider who is precise before any money changes hands tends to stay precise afterwards, and one who is vague has shown you how month three will feel.

whyPoints.description: Concepts, question recognition and diagnosis go in the paid hour; fluency goes into fifteen-minute daily drills. Reversing that split is the most common way a single weekly hour is wasted, and it is invisible because the session still feels productive.

whyPoints.title: A drill plan specific to the course
whyPoints.description: Analysis and Approaches candidates drill exact values and surds because Paper 1 has no calculator. Applications and Interpretation candidates drill statistical output reading and written justification. A single algebra sheet for both is a plan nobody built.

whyPoints.description: Twenty per cent of the grade, decomposed into topic stress-test, data check, one technique, one criterion at a time. That is what makes it survivable in a week with a long bus route and no spare weekends.

faqs.question: Is one hour a week enough for IB maths?
faqs.answer: Enough, if the hour is spent on what needs a teacher and the student drills daily. The hour should go on concepts that have not landed, recognising what questions ask for, and diagnosis from a marked script. Fluency work, meaning algebraic rearrangement, surds, exact values and mental estimation, improves with fifteen minutes a day and barely at all with sixty minutes a week, because the gain depends on frequency. Families who spend the hour on fluency get a session that feels productive and leaves the real blockage untouched for another week.

faqs.question: What should a daily maths drill actually contain?
faqs.answer: Fifteen minutes, in three blocks, with the content fixed for a fortnight so there is nothing to decide each evening. Five minutes of speed arithmetic and algebra. Five minutes on one weakness the tutor has set. Five minutes on a single past-paper question against a timer. On a bad evening, do the speed block alone rather than nothing, which protects the habit. The tutor's role is to read the week's errors at the start of each session and reset the second block fortnightly, which turns the drill into diagnosis.

faqs.question: Where do the withheld marks go on a Diploma calculator paper?
faqs.answer: Because the method is not visible. On a calculator paper a student solves something on screen and writes the result, which collects the answer mark and forfeits the method marks, often the larger share on a multi-part question. Writing the equation or integral being evaluated before producing the value takes a few seconds and recovers them. The other common causes are rounding at an intermediate step, retyping a previous result rather than storing it, and giving an answer in the wrong form or to the wrong accuracy.

faqs.question: Does Analysis and Approaches really need calculator-free practice?
faqs.answer: Yes, because Paper 1 is sat without a calculator at both levels of that course. Exact-value arithmetic, surd handling and fraction fluency stop being good habits and become examination requirements. A student who can perform every technique slowly will meet Paper 1 unable to finish, and in a calculator-free paper slowness is indistinguishable from not knowing. That work belongs in the daily drill rather than the weekly hour, because it is repetition rather than explanation and it decays within a week without contact.

faqs.question: How do we fit the maths exploration into a full week?
faqs.answer: By refusing to treat it as a project. Broken into tasks it is a sequence of short decisions: test whether the topic can generate mathematics at the course level, secure the data or context, perform one analysis technique, draft one section, address one criterion. Most of those fit a thirty-minute evening. The only task that cannot be rushed is the topic test, because a topic that cannot reach the course level caps criterion E permanently and no later work recovers it.

faqs.question: Can a tutor work on the exploration without crossing a line?
faqs.answer: Yes, within clear limits that any provider should state before you ask. A tutor may teach what each criterion credits and how many marks it carries, stress-test a topic before weeks go into it, question a method until the student finds the weakness, model a technique on entirely different data, mark drafts against the descriptors and check referencing. A tutor may not write, draft, rewrite or edit any part of the submission at any price. One provider in UAE search results sells completed Internal Assessments, and the student carries all of that risk.

faqs.question: What is the best use of the eight weeks after a mock?
faqs.answer: Target the largest recoverable cluster from the script in the first fortnight, add a full timed paper in the second, then re-diagnose in week five rather than simply continuing. The last three weeks go on timing, question selection and finishing, with nothing new introduced after week six because a topic met in the final fortnight is a liability. Eight weeks will move specific marks if the plan comes from the script; it will not re-teach a course, and attempting that is how families cover everything and improve nothing.

faqs.question: Does Paper 3 fit into a normal weekly hour?
faqs.answer: No, and that is the one task on this page where the hour is genuinely the wrong container. A Higher Level Paper 3 investigation takes longer than sixty minutes to attempt and then review properly, so squeezing it in means either an incomplete attempt or no review. Schedule it as a two-hour weekend or late-evening double, as a short block of four to six sessions in the term before the session, and work on recovering from an early error rather than only on avoiding one.

faqs.question: My child is slow rather than confused. What does that need?
faqs.answer: Daily repetition, not more teaching. Slowness in routine manipulation is a fluency problem, and fluency responds to fifteen minutes a day and almost nothing to a weekly lesson. A tutor's useful contribution is to identify precisely which operations are slow, set a fortnight of targeted drill, and read the error pattern each week. Buying extra tutoring hours for a fluency problem is the most expensive way to solve it, and it is what happens when nobody separates the two kinds of difficulty.

faqs.question: Can we find a Higher Level maths tutor who will come to Al Reef?
faqs.answer: In practice, rarely, and the reason is arithmetic rather than reputation. A tutor driving out past the airport road on a weekday evening commits most of that evening to one paid hour, so the few who will do it are selected by willingness to travel rather than by syllabus knowledge. Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level is the thinnest Diploma course to staff anywhere in the emirate. IB Gram does not offer home visits in the UAE at all; lessons run over live video, matched on the course taught.

faqs.question: How do we know which of the four maths courses my child takes?
faqs.answer: Ask the school and get it in writing: Analysis and Approaches or Applications and Interpretation, Higher or Standard Level. It changes the content depth, the calculator rules, whether a third paper is sat, and what the daily drill should contain. A tutor who produces the same drill sheet regardless of the answer has not built a plan for your child. Somebody teaching the course specifies different daily practice for Analysis and Approaches than for Applications and Interpretation, and can say why.

faqs.question: Should a parent supervise the daily drill?
faqs.answer: Collect it, do not teach it. The plan works because it needs no decisions and no explanation: fixed content for a fortnight, three five-minute blocks, written on a card or a shared note. A parent's role is to make sure the week's work reaches the session, which is what converts practice into diagnosis. Trying to mark it or explain it usually ends in an argument and in a parent teaching a method that differs from the school's, which creates a problem rather than solving one.

faqs.question: What if the weekly slot keeps getting cancelled?
faqs.answer: Move it after the second cancellation rather than defending it. Al Reef routes are long and variable, and a slot chosen for a good week collapses in a normal one. Because nobody is travelling to the house, a weekly time can shift to a later evening or another day in a single message, and the tutor loses nothing. The arrangements that fail are the ones where a family keeps a broken slot out of politeness, misses three sessions and then stops without saying why.

faqs.question: Is it worth starting in the final term of Year 13?
faqs.answer: Yes, with a changed aim. By then content teaching is largely over and the recoverable marks are the ones being withheld rather than missed: invisible method on calculator papers, answers in the wrong form, abandoned questions that were nearly finished. Take a marked mock, count the marks lost on questions where the answer was broadly right, and that figure is roughly what technique work can recover in eight or ten weeks. It is a smaller ambition than a course rescue and a far more achievable one.

faqs.question: How quickly can a match be arranged from Al Reef?
faqs.answer: Applications and Interpretation at either level and Analysis and Approaches at Standard Level usually match within a few days, because online delivery means the pool is not limited to tutors willing to drive out here. Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level can take a week or more, and it tightens around school internal deadlines when every Diploma cohort in the corridor needs the same help. You are told which applies before the trial, along with where the tutor is based and the time zone the session is set to.

Then take the free trial hour over live video, with no card details, and ask your child whether they followed it.

abu-dhabi/ib-maths-tutor-in-al-reem-isla.tutorsIntro: The tutors below teach IB Diploma mathematics to Abu Dhabi students, including families across Al Reem Island. Each works in one of the four routes rather than all of them, and each plans a block against your school's own deadline calendar rather than against a generic revision timetable.

intro.heading: Diploma mathematics is a two-year calendar, not a subject
paragraphs: Every Diploma maths problem a family brings us has a date attached to it, and the date determines the answer more than the problem does. A DP1 student struggling with differentiation in November has eighteen months and should fix the underlying algebra. A DP2 student in the same position in February has eleven weeks and should be practising papers while patching selectively. Same symptom, opposite prescriptions, and a tutor who does not ask the date will get one of them wrong.

The calendar has four fixed points. The school's internal deadline for the exploration, which arrives earlier in DP2 than most families expect. The mock examinations, which are the first honest read on where a student will land. The May session itself, which UAE Diploma schools sit. And results, after which a small number of decisions become available and then close quickly. Everything useful in Diploma maths tutoring is scheduled against those four points.

The most common error is not laziness, it is sequencing. Families buy weekly content tutoring from the first term of DP1 and continue it unchanged for two years, which spends the budget evenly across a course whose demands are anything but even. The first year is mostly content the school is covering at the same time, so a paid hour adds little. The second year is internal assessment and technique, where the school has limited time and a paid hour adds a great deal.

There is also a quieter error, which is treating the exploration as a DP2 problem. It is assessed in DP2 and it is planned in DP1. A student who has never thought about a topic until the term it is due will produce something inside the page range and well below their capability, because the criteria reward personal engagement and genuine reflection, and neither of those can be manufactured in a fortnight. Twenty per cent of the grade sits there.

Al Reem Island families have one practical advantage worth using: the island's Diploma cohort is concentrated across a handful of campuses, so the internal deadline calendar is knowable. Ask the school in the first term of DP2 for the exploration deadline, the mock window and the Extended Essay dates in writing, and the whole plan can be drawn backwards from them in an afternoon.

What follows is that plan. The Diploma maths year term by term, the exploration counted backwards from its internal deadline, an eight-week run-in set out week by week, what changes when Ramadan falls inside the revision window, and how the Al Reem Island school day constrains the slot. This page publishes no IB session or results dates, because none has been confirmed from the IB's own site; those come from your school's coordinator.

abu-dhabi/ib-maths-tutor-in-al-reem-isla.programmesIntro: The calendar differs by programme as much as the content does. These are the stages behind a Diploma maths enquiry from an Al Reem Island household, with what each stage's timetable actually demands.

programmes.name: IB Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Two years, six subjects, three at higher level, plus Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and Creativity, Activity, Service. Mathematics is compulsory. The maths calendar runs content through DP1 and the first term of DP2, the exploration across the middle, and technique in the final two terms, with mocks as the pivot between the second and third phases.
programmes.countryNote: UAE Diploma schools sit the May session, and Abu Dhabi private schools are licensed and inspected by ADEK. No IB session or results date appears on this page: the IB's own site blocks automated access, nothing has been confirmed at source, and a date a family plans around has to come from the school's IB coordinator.

programmes.name: IB Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Criterion-assessed with four criteria per subject rather than terminal papers, which means the MYP calendar has no single high-stakes window. The consequence for maths is a student who arrives in DP1 with strong grades and no experience of sitting a timed non-calculator paper. That gap is best closed in the summer between MYP and DP1, which almost nobody uses.
programmes.countryNote: Abu Dhabi has both continuum schools and Diploma-only schools, so a DP1 maths class in this emirate mixes Middle Years Programme leavers with International GCSE leavers. The two groups need different first terms, and the calendar is the reason: one group needs exam behaviour, the other needs content depth.

programmes.name: The International GCSE route into DP maths
programmes.description: Students arriving from Cambridge or Pearson Edexcel International GCSE have sat terminal papers and have the exam behaviour the Diploma assumes. What they often lack is the algebraic fluency that Analysis and Approaches at higher level demands from the first month. Cambridge Additional Mathematics 0606, where a school offers it, closes most of that gap a year early.
programmes.countryNote: The cheapest Diploma maths tutoring a family will ever buy is a short block in the summer between Year 11 and DP1, aimed at algebraic fluency. Remediation at the same depth in DP2 costs several times as much and competes with the exploration and five other subjects.

programmes.name: The Diploma core and the calendar collision
programmes.description: The Extended Essay and Theory of Knowledge essay have their own internal deadlines, and in most schools they land close to the maths exploration deadline. That collision is the single most predictable crisis in DP2 and the easiest to avoid, because all three dates are knowable in the first term of the year.
programmes.countryNote: Ask your school for all three internal deadlines together rather than one at a time. Al Reem Island families whose children attend the same few campuses can usually compare notes, and a family who maps the collision in September spends DP2 differently from one who discovers it in January.

abu-dhabi/ib-maths-tutor-in-al-reem-isla.subjectsIntro: Mathematics is the subject, but the calendar is shared with five others. These entries name each subject's own pressure point so a household can see where the maths block has to fit.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: Two papers at standard level weighted 40 per cent each; three at higher level weighted 30, 30 and 20, with the exploration at 20 per cent throughout. Paper 1 is sat without a calculator, and the fluency it assumes takes months rather than weeks to build, which makes it a DP1 job.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: Same paper structure and exploration weighting, with a calculator permitted on every paper. The calendar difference is that interpretation practice can be compressed late more successfully than non-calculator fluency can, which slightly changes how a short run-in should be spent.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.description: The scientific investigation deadline usually sits near the maths exploration deadline, which is the collision most families meet first. Physics also depends on the algebra that maths Paper 1 trains, so a DP1 fluency block pays into two subjects.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: The internal investigation needs laboratory time the school controls, so its timeline is less flexible than the maths exploration's. Where both fall in the same term, the chemistry work has to be sequenced first and the maths exploration planned around it.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.description: The highest content volume in the Diploma, which makes it the subject that absorbs revision time in the final weeks. A household planning a maths run-in has to account for that, because the student's total available hours are fixed.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.description: The portfolio of commentaries is written across the course rather than in one block, which makes it the least disruptive internal component to schedule and the easiest to leave too late. Each commentary has its own word limit.

subjects.name: English A
subjects.description: The individual oral is a scheduled event rather than a deadline, and schools set it where it suits the department. It is fully knowable in advance, which makes it the easiest component in the Diploma to prepare properly and a common casualty of poor sequencing.

subjects.name: History and Geography
subjects.description: Both carry an internal investigation with a stated word limit, and in several schools those deadlines cluster with the maths exploration. Source evaluation and fieldwork methodology are their own marked sections and need their own time.

subjects.name: Theory of Knowledge
subjects.description: A 1,600-word essay on a prescribed title plus an exhibition of around 950 words. Internal deadlines sit well before external ones, and in most schools the essay lands in the same term as the maths exploration.

subjects.name: Extended Essay
subjects.description: Up to 4,000 words with a school supervisor and a staged internal timetable of drafts. The staging is the point: a school that requires a first full draft by a given date has effectively set the real deadline months before the submission one.

subjects.name: Arabic
subjects.description: Required alongside the licensed international curriculum under federal rules covering Arabic, social studies and Islamic studies, and timetabled by the school. Relevant to the calendar because it occupies hours a family planning revision often forgets to count.

sections.heading: The Diploma maths calendar, term by term
paragraphs: Mapped across two years, Diploma mathematics has five phases and each one has a different job. Treating them identically is the sequencing error that costs families the most money, because it spends evenly on a course that demands unevenly.

DP1 autumn is settling and content. The school is teaching the first topics, the student is adjusting to a timed non-calculator paper if they came from the Middle Years Programme, and the only tutoring with real marginal value is diagnostic or fluency work. DP1 spring is the fluency window proper: the point at which algebraic automaticity can still be built without competing with anything else. DP1 summer, which almost nobody uses, is where the exploration topic should be chosen and tested.

DP2 autumn is internal assessment season. The exploration deadline, the Extended Essay drafts and the Theory of Knowledge essay typically land in this term or just after it, and they collide. This is where a bounded coaching block earns more per hour than at any other point in the two years, because the criteria are published, the deadline is fixed, and twenty per cent of the maths grade is at stake. DP2 spring is mocks and then the run-in, which is paper discipline rather than content.

The table sets the phases out with the job each one has and the failure that follows from skipping it. Confirm the specific dates with your school's IB coordinator, because internal deadlines are set per campus and the external calendar is not restated here.

sections.heading: The exploration, counted backwards from the school's deadline
paragraphs: The exploration carries twenty per cent of the maths grade, is marked out of twenty across five criteria, and has a school internal deadline that sits well before anything external. Counting backwards from that internal date is the only sensible way to plan it, and it produces a timeline longer than most students expect.

Work back from submission. Before submission there is a final check against each criterion, which takes a session. Before that there is a full draft the student has written, which takes weeks rather than days if the mathematics is genuinely theirs. Before that there is the mathematics itself, worked and verified, which is where the six marks for use of mathematics are won or lost. Before that there is a tested topic, which means a topic with enough mathematics in it to reach the top band and a genuine link to the student. And before all of it there is reading the criteria, which takes twenty minutes and is skipped by a majority of candidates.

Laid out that way, the exploration needs the whole of a term rather than a fortnight, and it needs to start in the term before the deadline. A student beginning four weeks out will produce something within the page range that scores in the middle band, because personal engagement and reflection cannot be retrofitted and use of mathematics cannot be pitched upwards at the last minute without the maths becoming someone else's.

That last point is the boundary. A tutor may explain each criterion and its mark allocation, test whether a topic the student proposed can reach the top band, teach the techniques the student has chosen to use, and give feedback on a draft the student wrote. No tutor may write the exploration, rewrite a draft into its final form, or supply text for submission. One page competing for these searches sells completed internal assessments outright, which risks the student's Diploma rather than the provider's business.

sections.heading: The eight-week run-in, week by week
paragraphs: After the mocks there is a finite number of weeks and a finite number of sessions, and the difference between a good run-in and a bad one is almost entirely structure. A bad run-in does more of what the student already does. A good one is a loop: sit a paper under conditions, mark it together against the published scheme, name the reason for every lost mark, patch the top two topics, repeat.

Eight weeks at two sessions a week is sixteen sessions, which at ninety minutes each is enough for roughly six full papers with their marking plus a handful of targeted repair sessions. That arithmetic is worth doing in advance, because it tells a family how many papers can realistically be covered and therefore which components to prioritise. At higher level, Paper 3 has to be allocated its own share or it gets squeezed out.

The ranked topic list is the artefact that makes the loop work. After each marked paper it is updated, and across eight weeks it should visibly shorten. If it does not, something is wrong with the diagnosis rather than with the student's effort, and the plan should change rather than continue. This is the measurable thing a parent should ask about, and it is a far better question than asking how revision is going.

The week-by-week table below is a template rather than a prescription. Shift it to fit your school's mock dates and the student's other subjects, which in the final term are competing for the same hours. The structure is what matters: papers under conditions, marking as the main event, and repair driven by the list rather than by whatever felt difficult.

sections.heading: When Ramadan falls inside the revision window
paragraphs: Ramadan moves approximately eleven days earlier each year against the Gregorian calendar, which means that over a run of years it passes through the whole of the academic year and spends several of those years sitting inside the spring term. For a DP2 student in Abu Dhabi that can place it squarely in the run-in to the May session, and a revision plan that ignores it will simply not be followed.

The practical adjustments are straightforward once they are planned rather than improvised. School days are shortened during Ramadan, which changes arrival times home and therefore the session window. Energy in the late afternoon is lower, which makes a ninety-minute timed paper at 17:00 a poor use of a session. Post-Iftar timing works far better for demanding work, and because lessons are delivered over live video, moving a session to a later evening slot costs nothing and requires no journey from anyone.

There is a sequencing opportunity here as well. The parts of a run-in that need peak concentration are the timed papers; the parts that need less are the review and the lighter repair work. A plan that puts papers in post-Iftar slots and review in the shortened afternoons gets more out of the month than one that keeps the same timetable and quietly delivers less in every session.

Eid then interrupts the following week or two, and schools and families both travel. A run-in built with that break accounted for is a run-in that survives. One built as eight consecutive weeks of two sessions will lose a fortnight and arrive at the May session two papers short, which is the sort of avoidable shortfall that shows up in a result and gets attributed to the student.
bullets: Ramadan shifts about eleven days earlier each year, so it passes through the spring term periodically
Shortened school days change when a session can start
Put timed papers in post-Iftar slots and review in the afternoons
Build the Eid break into the run-in rather than discovering it

sections.heading: The components in the final weeks, and which deserve the time
paragraphs: At standard level there are two papers weighted forty per cent each; at higher level there are three weighted thirty, thirty and twenty. The exploration carries twenty per cent at both levels and is finished by the time the run-in starts, which simplifies the final weeks: all remaining effort goes to papers, and the allocation between them should follow the weighting and the student's measured weakness rather than habit.

Paper 1 in Analysis and Approaches is sat without a calculator and is where classwork and exam performance diverge most, because students who have worked with a screen in front of them have never built the arithmetic fluency the paper assumes. In a late run-in this is only partially fixable, which is exactly why the DP1 spring fluency block matters so much. What can be done late is timing: measuring how long the paper actually takes without a calculator and adjusting question order accordingly.

Paper 3 at higher level is an extended problem-solving investigation and is the component most often squeezed out of a run-in, because it is uncomfortable and the mathematics in it is familiar enough that students assume it needs no separate work. It does. The difficulty is structural rather than mathematical: following the thread of a multi-part investigation under time pressure is a practised skill, and twenty per cent of the grade sits there.

Applications and Interpretation changes the emphasis slightly. With a calculator permitted throughout, the late-run-in gains sit in interpretation and in method recording: giving a number and then saying what it means in the context the question described, and showing the steps rather than only the output. Both respond well to compressed practice, which makes a short AI run-in more productive per week than a short AA one.
bullets: Allocate run-in time by component weighting and measured weakness, not by preference
Paper 1 timing can be fixed late; Paper 1 fluency cannot
Paper 3 at higher level needs its own allocated share of the run-in

sections.heading: Where the calendar goes wrong
paragraphs: Four failures recur, and all four are scheduling rather than ability. The first is the flat two-year weekly arrangement, which spends the budget evenly across a course with uneven demands and leaves nothing for the phases where a paid hour is worth most. Families rarely plan this; they arrive at it by starting a weekly session in DP1 and never revisiting the decision.

The second is discovering the internal deadlines late. School deadlines for the exploration, the Extended Essay and the Theory of Knowledge essay sit well before external ones and in most schools they cluster. A family that gets all three in writing in the first term of DP2 can sequence them. A family that meets them one at a time in January cannot, and the maths exploration is usually the component that gives way because it feels the most self-contained.

The third is starting the run-in after the mocks are returned. By then the calendar has closed in: there may be six weeks rather than eight, other subjects are competing, and the student is tired. The run-in has to be booked during the spring term as a decision, not assembled reactively from whatever time is left.

The fourth is continuing to pay after the work is done. The honest end of a bounded block is the end of the block, and the honest end of a run-in is the examination. A weekly arrangement that drifts past its purpose is the most expensive thing in this market, and it is sustained by the fact that comfortable sessions feel like progress. The test is whether the ranked topic list is still shortening. If it is empty, stop.
bullets: Revisit a weekly arrangement at every half term rather than letting it run
Get all internal deadlines in writing in the first term of DP2
Book the run-in during the spring term, before the mocks are returned
Stop when the ranked topic list is empty; comfortable sessions are not progress

sections.heading: Fitting the plan into an Al Reem Island evening
paragraphs: A calendar plan only works if the sessions in it can actually happen. Campuses serving Al Reem Island finish their taught day between about 14:45 and 15:30, with co-curricular sessions later on some days. A student at a campus on or near the island is often home by 15:50; a student commuting to the Khalifa City or Al Raha corridor is typically not home before 16:15, and later still on an activity day.

Allowing three quarters of an hour at home, that puts the honest earliest start at 16:30 for a nearby campus and 17:30 for a mainland commute. Our Abu Dhabi scheduling range runs from 16:30 to 21:00 Gulf Standard Time. Across a two-year plan the slots that survive are the ones at 18:00 and 18:30, because a slot that only works on an untroubled week will break inside a fortnight and a broken slot is a missed phase of the plan.

Session length should follow the phase. The run-in needs ninety minutes, because the working unit is a paper plus its marking. Exploration coaching works in sixty, since the material is the student's own draft. A DP1 fluency block works in sixty or even forty-five, because non-calculator drills are better short and frequent than long and occasional. Choosing the length before choosing the purpose is a common and avoidable waste.

Because lessons are delivered one-to-one over live video, a late school finish moves a session rather than cancelling it, and a family travelling over a half term keeps the plan with a time-zone adjustment. IB Gram does not offer home visits anywhere in the UAE; that is an India-only service. For context, published market bands put in-home one-to-one at AED 180-500 an hour against AED 150-300 for a qualified tutor working online, with Bestimate quoting AED 180-350 for in-home work and Unitors listing IB tuition from AED 200. Those are market figures from the sources named, not our prices.
