sections.heading: Structure, register and the referencing marks nobody teaches
paragraphs: Criterion C is the cheapest level in the subject group and the most frequently abandoned. Three strands: style appropriate to audience and purpose, structure appropriate to the specified format, and sources documented using a recognised convention. All three are mechanical, all three are teachable in a handful of sessions, and none of them depends on the student becoming cleverer.

Format is where Abu Dhabi students lose ground first, because MYP humanities tasks are set in many shapes: a report, an essay, a newspaper article, a presentation, a letter, an infographic. Each has conventions, and a student who writes an essay when a report was asked for has ignored a strand of the criterion. The fix is to read the task sheet for the format and then plan to that shape before writing. Thirty seconds of reading saves a level.

Referencing is the single most wasted mark in the group. The strand asks only for a recognised convention applied consistently. It does not care which one, provided the school has not specified. A student who picks one, uses it for in-text citations and builds a matching reference list has secured those marks regardless of the quality of their argument. Instead, students commonly paste a bare web address, or reference nothing, or mix three styles. Setting up a recording template at the start of an investigation, so that the reference exists at the moment the source is read, removes the problem entirely and takes ten minutes.

sections.heading: The on-screen examination, and what it changes about preparation
paragraphs: Some Abu Dhabi schools enter MYP 5 students for the IB's on-screen examinations, and individuals and societies is one of the subjects available as an integrated humanities paper. Where a school does enter candidates, the preparation changes character: the assessment is externally set and marked, it uses unseen sources, and it is sat on screen under timed conditions rather than produced over weeks.

That shifts what is worth practising. Criterion B's investigation strands matter less in an examination that supplies the material, and criterion D matters more, because the student is handed sources they have never seen and asked to use them under time pressure. Students who have only ever evaluated sources they chose themselves, with the internet open, find this hard. Sessions therefore move to timed source work: short passages, a clock, and a written judgement in a fixed number of minutes.

The on-screen format itself needs rehearsal. Typing rather than handwriting changes planning habits, sources have to be read in a window rather than on paper, and there is no margin to annotate in. Students who are fluent writers on paper sometimes lose structure on screen simply because they cannot see the whole answer at once. Two or three timed rehearsals in the actual format remove most of that penalty. Whether your child's school enters candidates at all is a school decision, so ask the MYP coordinator rather than assuming either way; plenty of excellent MYP schools do not.

sections.heading: What one session fixes, and the honesty line in a research subject
paragraphs: In a single fifty-minute session a humanities tutor can do a small number of genuinely useful things. They can narrow a research question from unanswerable to answerable, which changes the whole investigation. They can set up a citation convention and a recording template, securing criterion C's third strand permanently. They can read a marked essay and name which criterion strand lost the level. Or they can run one source-evaluation drill that shifts how the student reads everything afterwards.

What one session cannot do is build critical thinking, teach a term of content or move a grade. Criterion D takes four to eight sessions for a level, because it is a habit rather than a technique. Being clear about that before any money changes hands prevents the most common complaint in this market, which is a family who bought three sessions expecting a transformation and received three sessions.

The honesty line matters more in a research subject than almost anywhere else, because the raw material is text and the temptation is obvious. A tutor may teach research method, discuss what makes a question answerable, question a student's reasoning, mark practice work, explain a citation convention and show how to judge an unfamiliar source. A tutor may not supply paragraphs for a submission, choose and summarise the sources on the student's behalf, or edit a draft into a finished state. The practical test is whether the student could explain every sentence and defend every source choice if their teacher asked. Work the student genuinely produced survives that; work produced for them does not, and the student is the one who carries the consequence.

sections.heading: Where MYP humanities leads, and what the UAE requires later
paragraphs: The skills in this subject group have the longest reach of anything in the MYP. Criterion B is the Extended Essay in miniature: a focused question, a justified relevance, a plan, sources, and an evaluation of the process. Criterion D is the analytical core of Diploma history and the reasoning demand in economics, geography and global politics. Criterion C's referencing strand is simply how academic work is done, and a student who has internalised one convention at fourteen never has to think about it again.

Parents in this emirate also ask how any of this connects to UAE Ministry of Education equivalency, which matters for university admission locally. The published British-track requirement is specific: proof of one accredited subject at Advanced Level with a grade of no less than E, or two accredited subjects at Advanced Subsidiary Level at the same grade, together with five accredited subjects at GCSE or IGCSE with a grade of no less than E or grade 3. Arabic and Islamic education are not included among those five required subjects. One ranking competitor publishes a six-subject figure, which is wrong.

For IB students the honest answer is that we will not publish a points threshold, because no figure has been read on the Ministry's own pages and an unsourced number on a page like this is worse than silence. Equivalency and attestation are processes the authority runs, not something a tutoring provider performs or guarantees, and no part of it requires tutoring. Ask your school's university counsellor and check the Ministry's own guidance. What the MYP contributes is indirect and real: a student who can research, reference and argue arrives at the Diploma able to earn the grades the equivalency process will eventually look at.

process.title: Say which subject the task belongs to
process.description: MYP individuals and societies or federally required UAE social studies. The two are taught in different lessons under different rules, and a tutor who guesses wrong teaches the wrong thing. If you are unsure, the task sheet usually says, and the criterion rubric is the giveaway.

process.title: Send the task sheet and one marked piece
process.description: The task sheet names the format, the command terms and the criteria being assessed; the marked piece shows which strand lost the level. Together they usually identify the target in ten minutes, and the target is frequently criterion C, which nobody expects.

process.title: One session at no charge on real work
process.description: A fifty-minute session with a humanities specialist at no charge, one per family, no card details taken. It runs on your child's actual task, and where the task is an investigation it usually ends with a narrower research question than the one it started with.

process.title: Pick one criterion and a session count
process.description: Agreed in writing with the rate in AED, whether preparation time is charged, and the reschedule window. Criterion C can be a three-session job. Criterion D is a term. Buying them as though they were the same size is the usual mistake.

process.title: Review on marked practice work
process.description: Practice tasks are marked against the published strands, not given a percentage, so the review compares like with like. If the targeted strand has not moved after six weeks we say so and look at whether the obstacle is humanities, writing or the hour of the evening the session lands in.

whyPoints.title: The two-subject confusion cleared first
whyPoints.description: MYP individuals and societies and UAE social studies are different subjects with different rules, and conflating them produces timid content-recall writing that scores badly. Establishing which one a task belongs to is the first question we ask, and it changes what gets taught.

whyPoints.title: Criterion B taught as a document, not a pep talk
whyPoints.description: The research question is narrowed against a written test of answerability, the relevance is justified in a sentence that says something, and the action plan exists as a file with dates in it. Those are the strands students lose, and they are produced by the student in session.

whyPoints.title: Source work practised, not defined
whyPoints.description: Origin, purpose and value are useless as a definition and powerful as a habit. Sessions put four to six real sources in front of a student, including an unreliable one, and require a written judgement each time until the formula becomes thinking.

whyPoints.title: The cheapest level, taken first
whyPoints.description: Documenting sources in one recognised convention is a criterion C strand that depends on no insight whatsoever. We set up the convention and the recording template in the first session, because it is the fastest level available and almost everyone leaves it on the table.

whyPoints.title: A stated academic-honesty boundary
whyPoints.description: Tutors teach method, question reasoning and mark practice work. They do not supply paragraphs, select and summarise sources on a student's behalf, or edit a draft to completion. The test is whether the student could defend every sentence and source choice to their teacher.

whyPoints.title: No unsourced claims about equivalency
whyPoints.description: We publish the British-track equivalency requirements because they are sourced, and we decline to publish an IB points threshold because no figure has been read on the Ministry's own pages. Equivalency is the authority's process, not ours, and tutoring is not required for it.

faqs.question: What is the difference between MYP individuals and societies and UAE social studies?
faqs.answer: They are two different subjects studied side by side. MYP individuals and societies is an IB subject group covering history, geography, economics and related disciplines, assessed against four criteria on tasks your school writes. UAE social studies is federally required: private schools must follow Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies alongside their licensed curriculum, with prescribed content that cannot be supplemented without Ministry permission. In Dubai the KHDA sets out the detail of class organisation and language of instruction; in Abu Dhabi the licensing authority is ADEK, so confirm the local requirement with your school.

faqs.question: Which subjects sit inside MYP individuals and societies?
faqs.answer: The group can draw on history, geography, economics, business management, politics, civics, sociology, psychology, philosophy and anthropology. In MYP 1 to 3 most Abu Dhabi schools teach an integrated humanities course, usually weighted towards history and geography. From MYP 4 schools may offer discrete named courses, and which ones depends entirely on the school. Ask for the unit planner rather than assuming: two students in the same year at different schools in this emirate can be studying an economics course and a history course under the same subject-group heading.

faqs.question: My son writes long, fluent essays and still gets a 4. Why?
faqs.answer: Almost always because he is writing to criterion A and being marked on criterion D. Fluent description of what happened demonstrates knowledge and understanding, which is one criterion out of four. Thinking critically asks for something different: a valid argument synthesised from information, sources evaluated by origin, purpose and value, and more than one perspective interpreted. A student who takes every source at face value and presents one view confidently will stall in the middle however well they write. Ask for the criterion levels separately and the pattern usually shows immediately.

faqs.question: How do we write a research question that actually works?
faqs.answer: Test it three ways. Can it be answered in the words available? Does it require weighing something rather than listing? Does it name a place, time or group so evidence exists about that specific thing? 'How does tourism affect Abu Dhabi' fails all three. 'To what extent has visitor growth on Saadiyat Island changed local employment patterns since 2015' passes all three, and it makes source work possible because real material exists about a defined subject. Narrowing a question is usually a one-session job and it improves every later part of the investigation.

faqs.question: What does criterion D, thinking critically, actually want?
faqs.answer: Four things, stated in its strands. Discussing concepts, issues, models and theories rather than only events. Synthesising information into a valid argument, so the conclusion follows from the evidence. Analysing and evaluating sources in terms of origin, purpose and value, which means saying what each source can and cannot support. And interpreting different perspectives and their implications, which means engaging with the serious version of the opposing view. None of this is about having opinions. It is about handling evidence, and it takes four to eight sessions to build as a habit.

faqs.question: How should an MYP student evaluate a source properly?
faqs.answer: By drawing consequences from the origin and purpose rather than just stating them. A government publication about a development project knows things nobody outside knows and has reason to present them favourably, so it is reliable about the figures it collected and selective about which figures appear. A news report from the week of an event is good evidence of reaction and cannot know the outcome. The level-7 move is a sentence that says what a source is good for and what it is not. That comes from practising on many sources, including unreliable ones, rather than from a definition.

faqs.question: Does referencing really earn marks in MYP individuals and societies?
faqs.answer: Yes, directly. Criterion C includes a strand on documenting sources using a recognised convention, and it does not specify which convention unless your school does. A student who picks one, uses it for in-text citations and builds a matching reference list secures those marks regardless of the quality of their argument. It is the cheapest level in the subject group and the most commonly abandoned: students paste bare web addresses, reference nothing, or mix three styles in one piece. Setting up a recording template at the start of an investigation solves it permanently.

faqs.question: What is the MYP on-screen humanities examination like?
faqs.answer: Where a school enters MYP 5 candidates, the integrated humanities paper is externally set and marked, uses unseen sources and is sat on screen under timed conditions. That rebalances preparation: the investigation strands of criterion B matter less when the material is supplied, and criterion D matters much more, because the student must evaluate sources they have never seen against a clock. Typing rather than handwriting also changes planning habits. Two or three timed rehearsals in the real format remove most of the penalty. Ask your coordinator whether your school enters candidates at all.

faqs.question: Is MYP individuals and societies good preparation for Diploma history or economics?
faqs.answer: The skills transfer better than the content. Criterion B is a small Extended Essay: a focused question, justified relevance, an action plan, sources and a process evaluation. Criterion D is the analytical core of Diploma history and the reasoning demand in economics and geography. Criterion C's referencing strand is simply how academic work is done. Content transfers much less, because MYP units are chosen by your school rather than prescribed. A student who leaves MYP 5 able to narrow a question and judge a source arrives in DP 1 with the hard part already in place.

faqs.question: Does my child need to memorise dates and facts for this subject?
faqs.answer: Less than parents expect, and more than students hope. Criterion A rewards knowledge demonstrated through descriptions, explanations and examples, so specific instances are needed; a student who cannot name a single example will not score well. What is not rewarded is recall for its own sake. A date with no significance attached earns nothing, while a precisely used example that supports an argument earns on two criteria at once. The practical approach is to learn fewer examples in more depth, which also makes criterion D far easier to write.

faqs.question: How many sessions does a humanities investigation take to support?
faqs.answer: For one full investigation taught end to end, plan on four to six sessions spread across the time the school has allowed. Session one narrows the question and justifies its relevance. Session two builds the action plan and the recording template. Sessions three and four work on source evaluation and the argument. A final session covers the process evaluation, which students almost always omit because they think the essay was the task. Compressing that into two sessions produces a tidier essay and no learning, and the next investigation starts from the same place.

faqs.question: Can a tutor help with the research for an individuals and societies investigation?
faqs.answer: With the method, yes. With the research itself, no. A tutor can teach how to search, how to judge what turns up, how to record a source so it can be cited, and how to decide whether material is relevant to the question. A tutor cannot select and summarise the sources on the student's behalf, supply paragraphs, or edit a draft into a finished state. The test is whether your child could explain every sentence and defend every source choice if their teacher asked on the spot. Work the student produced survives that conversation.

faqs.question: Do Arabic and Islamic education overlap with individuals and societies in Abu Dhabi?
faqs.answer: They sit alongside it rather than overlapping. Private schools in the UAE must follow Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies in addition to their licensed curriculum, and the KHDA's Dubai guidance requires separate classes for Arab and non-Arab students with specified languages of instruction. Abu Dhabi schools are licensed and inspected by ADEK, so check the local detail with your school. The practical effect on a tutoring plan is timetable pressure rather than content overlap: those lessons and their homework occupy evenings, so one protected weekly session beats an ambitious schedule.

faqs.question: Does MYP humanities count towards UAE Ministry of Education equivalency?
faqs.answer: The MYP itself is not what the equivalency process examines, and we will not publish an IB points threshold because no such figure has been read on the Ministry's own pages. What is sourced is the British track: five accredited subjects at GCSE or IGCSE at no less than grade E or grade 3, with Arabic and Islamic education excluded from that count, plus one Advanced Level subject at E or two Advanced Subsidiary subjects at E. Equivalency is the authority's process, not something a tutor performs, and no part of it requires tutoring. Ask your school's counsellor and check the Ministry directly.

faqs.question: What can one humanities session realistically fix?
faqs.answer: A small number of high-leverage things. It can narrow an unanswerable research question into an answerable one, which changes the entire investigation. It can set up a citation convention and a recording template, securing a criterion C strand permanently. It can read a marked essay and name which strand lost the level, which stops a family buying the wrong term. Or it can run one source drill that changes how the student reads everything afterwards. What it cannot do is build critical thinking or move a grade; criterion D is four to eight sessions of habit-building.

faqs.question: Are humanities lessons delivered at an Abu Dhabi address or online?
faqs.answer: Online. IB Gram does not offer home visits in Abu Dhabi, and visiting tutors are a service we run only in India. Every UAE lesson is one to one, live over video, scheduled in Gulf Standard Time. For a research subject the format suits the work: sources open in a second window, a draft is annotated on a shared screen while the student watches, and a reference list is built and corrected live. It also means the tutor is chosen for how well they teach criterion D rather than for living a short drive away.

abu-dhabi/ib-myp-individuals-and-societi.closingHeading: Send the task sheet, and we will start with the question
abu-dhabi/ib-myp-individuals-and-societi.closingBody: The fastest way into this subject is the smallest one. Send the task sheet, one marked piece of work and the criterion rubric, and say whether the task belongs to MYP individuals and societies or to UAE social studies. A humanities specialist will read all three, name the strand that is costing levels, and run one fifty-minute session at no charge on that exact task. Where the task is an investigation, you will usually finish with a narrower research question, a recording template and a citation convention, which between them are worth more than a term of general essay advice.

intro.heading: Phases, four skills, and why the grade tells you so little
paragraphs: Language acquisition is the MYP subject group that confuses Abu Dhabi parents most reliably, and the confusion is structural rather than anyone's fault. The course is not organised by year. It is organised into six phases of proficiency, and a student is placed in the phase that matches their level in that language, so an MYP 4 student might sit in phase 2 for Mandarin and phase 5 for French at the same time. Phases 1 and 2 cover emergent communicators, 3 and 4 capable communicators, 5 and 6 proficient communicators. The level on the report is relative to the phase, not to the year group, which is why two students with identical grades can be at completely different standards.

The second thing to know is what is marked. There are four criteria, each out of eight, and in the current guide they are listening, reading, speaking and writing. Older documentation names the same four differently: comprehending spoken and visual text, comprehending written and visual text, communicating in response to spoken, written and visual text, and using language in spoken and written form. Some Abu Dhabi schools still use rubrics with the older wording. Ask which version appears on your child's rubric, because the strand descriptions differ in emphasis and a tutor working from the wrong one will aim at the wrong thing.

What follows from this is that a grade in language acquisition is nearly uninformative on its own. It averages four skills that develop at different rates and that respond to completely different teaching. The commonest Abu Dhabi profile we see is a confident speaker with weak listening: a student who converses happily, who cannot answer questions on a recorded conversation at normal speed, and whose grade comes out in the middle. The second commonest is the reverse: a student with good written accuracy who freezes in a speaking assessment. Those two need opposite terms.

So the first useful act is separating the four. Ask for the four criterion levels rather than the grade, and ask which phase the student is registered in. Those five pieces of information take one email to obtain and they determine everything about what should be bought. A student at phase 3 with listening at 3 and writing at 6 needs audio work, not grammar drills, and a provider who sells them grammar drills will produce a busy term and a static level.

Lessons are delivered one to one, live over video, in Gulf Standard Time. IB Gram does not offer home visits in Abu Dhabi; visiting tutors are a service we run only in India. Language teaching is the case where the online format is least of a compromise and arguably an advantage: audio and video play at full quality through the same channel the lesson runs on, speaking practice can be recorded and played back in the session, and a student can be matched with a tutor who teaches their language at their phase rather than with whoever teaches that language nearby.

Schools here are licensed and inspected by ADEK, which publishes its own ratings.

A student finishing in phase 4 or 5 is usually placed into language B; a student in phase 1 or 2 may be steered to ab initio in a different language entirely. subjects.name: French

subjects.name: Spanish

subjects.name: Mandarin
subjects.description: Character recognition and tones make this the slowest phase progression of the commonly offered languages. Reading and writing levels typically lag listening and speaking by a phase, and this gap is expected rather than remarkable.

subjects.name: German
subjects.description: Case and word order make written accuracy the limiting skill. Students frequently understand far more than they can produce correctly, which shows as a strong criterion B and a weaker criterion D on the same report.

subjects.description: The separate course for students working in the language of instruction at a near-native level, assessed on literary analysis rather than on the four skills. Which course a student takes is a school placement decision based on proficiency, not a choice.

subjects.description: Required for Arab students in UAE private schools and taught within language and literature rather than language acquisition. subjects.name: Individuals and societies
subjects.description: Booked alongside language work when a student's difficulty is comprehension of extended text rather than vocabulary. A student who cannot structure a written response in English will not structure one in French either, and the skill is shared.

sections.heading: Phases, not years: the one thing to establish before the first lesson
paragraphs: Everything in this subject depends on the phase, and a surprising number of families do not know which phase their child is in. A phase is a proficiency band, and six of them cover the whole route from no knowledge of a language to near-independent use. Phases 1 and 2 describe emergent communicators: short, simple exchanges on familiar topics in predictable contexts. Phases 3 and 4 describe capable communicators, able to handle more varied text types and less familiar material. Phases 5 and 6 describe proficient communicators approaching independent use, dealing with abstract content and inference.

A student's phase is set by the school, usually by a placement assessment when they join the language, and it moves when the school judges that it should. It is not tied to the year group. That means an MYP 5 student in phase 2 Arabic is not behind: they are correctly placed and being marked against phase 2 expectations. Conversely, an MYP 2 student in phase 5 French is being marked against a far more demanding standard than their year group would suggest, and a level of 5 there is a different achievement from a 5 in phase 2.

This is why a grade alone is misleading and why the first question any competent tutor asks is which phase. A level 6 in phase 2 and a level 6 in phase 5 require completely different teaching, and material pitched at the wrong phase either bores or drowns the student within two sessions. If the report does not state the phase, email the language teacher; they will know immediately, and the answer frequently surprises the household.

Phase movement is also worth understanding before it is hoped for. Moving within a phase, which means raising a criterion level, is a term of work. Moving between phases is usually a year or more, because a phase represents a substantial expansion of range. Families who expect a phase change in a term are disappointed by progress that was in fact normal, and families who expect nothing are sometimes surprised by a level moving in six weeks. The table sets out what each band expects.

sections.heading: The four criteria are the four skills, and they fail separately
paragraphs: In the current guide the criteria are listening, reading, speaking and writing, each marked out of eight at the student's phase. Older documentation, still in use on some Abu Dhabi school rubrics, names the same four as comprehending spoken and visual text, comprehending written and visual text, communicating in response to spoken, written and visual text, and using language in spoken and written form. Ask which wording your child's rubric uses; the emphasis differs and so does what a tutor should practise.

They fail independently, and the pattern on the report is the diagnosis. Strong speaking with weak listening is the most common profile we see in Abu Dhabi, and it has an obvious cause: students get far more practice producing language than following it at natural speed, and classroom speech is usually slowed and clearly articulated in a way real speech is not. Strong writing with weak speaking is the second pattern, and it is usually nerves plus lack of rehearsal rather than lack of language. Strong listening and speaking with weak reading and writing is the normal Mandarin and Arabic profile, because script is a separate skill.

What this means practically is that the right purchase is narrow. A student at phase 3 with listening at 3 and writing at 6 should be buying audio work, and will waste a term on grammar exercises however well taught they are. A student with the reverse profile needs text types and accuracy, and more conversation will not help. Asking for four criterion levels instead of a grade takes one email, and it is the difference between a term that moves something and a term that feels productive.

table.caption: THE FOUR CRITERIA AND WHERE ABU DHABI STUDENTS LOSE LEVELS
rows: Classroom speech is slower than real speech, so natural pace is never practised
Literal comprehension is fine; inference and implied meaning are not attempted
Rehearsed answers are fluent; unseen prompts produce fillers and stalling
Writing (using language in spoken and written form)
Text-type conventions ignored; the same errors repeat across every piece

sections.heading: Listening: the skill nobody buys and most students need
paragraphs: Criterion A is the most neglected purchase in language tutoring, for an understandable reason: it is tiring, unrewarding in the short term, and produces no document a parent can admire. It is also where most Abu Dhabi students lose their levels, because almost all of their exposure to the language has been at a speed chosen for learners.

The method that works is uncomfortable and simple. Short audio, thirty to ninety seconds, played at full natural speed from the first session, with no slowing down. First listen for the gist, second listen for specific information, third listen for the detail the student missed. Then, occasionally, transcription of ten seconds, which is the fastest way to discover that the student is not failing to understand vocabulary but failing to hear where one word ends and the next begins. That diagnosis changes the teaching entirely, because the fix is phonetic rather than lexical.

Visual text matters too, and students forget it is assessed. The criterion covers spoken and visual material, so an image, a chart or a video with on-screen text is legitimate assessment material, and inference from visual cues is part of what is marked. Students who have only ever practised with audio recordings are caught out by a task built around a short film or an advertisement.

Progress on listening is slow and then sudden. Four to eight sessions is realistic for one level, and for the first three of those a student will feel they are getting worse, because they are noticing how much they were previously missing. It is worth telling families that in advance, because the three-week point is where listening blocks get abandoned, usually just before they start to work.

sections.heading: Reading, speaking and the gap between fluent and accurate
paragraphs: Criterion B, reading, divides cleanly into two things: literal comprehension and inference. Most students in this emirate handle the first and avoid the second. Asked what the text says, they answer correctly. Asked what the writer implies, what the tone suggests, or how two texts differ in attitude, they either restate the literal content or guess. From phase 3 upwards inference is explicitly part of what is marked, and it is teachable by asking the same three questions of every text until they become automatic: what is stated, what is implied, and how do you know.

Criterion C, speaking, has the largest gap between what students practise and what they are assessed on. Classroom speaking is often rehearsed: a prepared presentation, a known topic, a script in the background. Assessment uses unseen prompts and follow-up questions, where the skill is handling the unexpected without stalling. Students who are fluent on prepared material and lost on an unseen prompt are not short of language; they are short of rehearsal with unpredictability in it.

Recording is what makes speaking improvable. A student who answers a prompt, hears the recording once, and answers again improves on the second attempt almost every time, and what they correct is rarely vocabulary. It is pace, fillers, and sentences abandoned halfway because the thought changed mid-clause. Three sessions of this changes how a student sounds more than a term of conversation practice, because conversation practice rarely includes the moment of listening back.

The interaction between fluency and accuracy is worth naming, because it drives a real decision. In phases 1 to 3, fluency should usually be prioritised: getting the student talking, accepting errors, building willingness. From phase 4 upwards, accuracy starts to bind, and a student who has been praised for fluent approximate speech for three years will plateau. A tutor's job at that point is to start correcting more than feels kind, which parents sometimes read as harshness and is in fact the only route out of a plateau.

sections.heading: Writing to a text type, and the error log that fixes repetition
paragraphs: Criterion D is where the phase shows most clearly, because each phase expects a wider range of text types. A blog post, an email, a letter, a diary entry, a brochure, an article, a speech, a review: each has conventions of layout, opening, register and closing, and a student who writes an essay when a letter was set has lost marks before the language is read. Students routinely ignore the text type because nobody told them it was assessed, and the fix is a single sheet listing the conventions for each type, consulted before writing.

Register is the second half of criterion D and the strand that separates phase 4 from phase 5. The same content addressed to a friend and to a school principal requires different forms, and in languages with formal and informal address the choice is grammatical as well as tonal. Students who have learned a language mostly through informal exchange default to the informal register everywhere, which reads as a vocabulary problem and is actually a register problem.

Accuracy is where an error log earns its keep. Most students make a small number of errors repeatedly: in French, agreement and tense; in German, case and word order; in Spanish, ser against estar and the subjunctive; in Arabic, script direction, definite articles and sentence structure. Writing those down in a running list, reviewed at the start of each session, makes the repetition visible to the student. It is low-effort and it works, because the problem with repeated errors is not that they are hard to fix but that nobody has noticed they are the same error. A term of error-log work typically removes half the recurring mistakes in a student's writing without a single grammar lecture.

sections.heading: Arabic as an additional language in this emirate
paragraphs: In Abu Dhabi, language acquisition frequently means Arabic, because private schools in the UAE must follow Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies alongside their licensed curriculum, with Arabic taken as a first language by Arab students and as an additional language by others. In Dubai the KHDA's mandatory-subjects guidance states that separate classes must be organised for Arabs and non-Arabs in Arabic as a first language, Islamic education and social studies, that combined classes are prohibited because the curriculum expectations and the language of instruction differ, and that schools must ensure all teachers of Islamic education and Arabic hold the appropriate KHDA approval to teach those subjects. It also sets instructional time against a forty-minute lesson unit and advises that no mandatory subject lesson should be shorter than twenty-five minutes. Abu Dhabi schools are licensed and inspected by ADEK, so confirm the local requirement with your school.

Progress in Arabic as an additional language is genuinely slower than in French or Spanish, and families should expect that rather than read it as failure. Three things account for it. The script is a separate skill from the spoken language, so reading and writing lag listening and speaking by a phase for most students. Standard Arabic, which is what is taught and assessed, differs from the spoken dialect a student hears around them, so out-of-class exposure helps less directly than it would in Spain. And sentence structure diverges enough from English that early sentences require real reconstruction rather than word substitution.

The compensating advantage is that Abu Dhabi supplies exposure free of charge, provided it is used deliberately. Signage, labels, numbers, greetings and short service exchanges are available every day, and a student who reads every sign they pass builds script recognition faster than any worksheet achieves. For families whose child is in phase 1 or 2 and frustrated, that is the intervention worth making first, before any tutoring: fifteen minutes a day of reading the environment, which costs nothing and moves script recognition measurably within a month.

sections.heading: The MYP 5 ePortfolio, and what it changes
paragraphs: Language acquisition is assessed differently from most MYP subjects in the final year. Where an Abu Dhabi school enters MYP 5 candidates for the IB's external assessment, language acquisition is submitted as a portfolio of work rather than sat as an on-screen examination, and the phase the student is registered in sets the standard the work is judged against. Whether your school enters candidates at all is a school decision, so ask the MYP coordinator rather than assuming either way.

Where it applies, the consequence is that the record matters more than a single performance. Portfolio work is produced across time, which rewards consistency and punishes a student who was coasting until March. It also means the text types produced during the year are not just practice; they are candidates for the submission. A student who has written three text types well and ignored the rest has a thinner portfolio than one who covered the range, regardless of raw ability.

The authorship rules are correspondingly strict, and this is where a tutor's boundary has to be explicit. Portfolio work must be the student's own. A tutor may teach the language, drill listening, rehearse speaking, mark practice work, explain a text type's conventions and keep an error log. A tutor may not write or rewrite a piece intended for submission, supply sentences, or translate the student's ideas into the target language for them. Translating for a student is the specific temptation in this subject, and it is the one that most clearly crosses the line, because the resulting text demonstrates nothing about the student at all. Teachers can and do ask students to talk through submitted work, and work the student produced survives that conversation while work produced for them does not.

process.title: Find out the phase
process.description: One email to the language teacher. Which phase is my child registered in, and which version of the criterion rubric does the school use? Those two answers decide the material, the pitch and the target, and the household frequently does not know either of them.

process.title: Ask for four levels, not a grade
process.description: Listening, reading, speaking and writing separately. The grade averages four skills that develop at different rates, so it hides the only information worth having. A student at 3 in listening and 6 in writing needs the opposite term from one with the reverse profile.

process.title: One session at no charge, diagnostic
process.description: A fifty-minute session with a language specialist at no charge, one per family, no card details taken. It tests all four skills briefly at the registered phase, including unseen audio and an unprepared speaking prompt, because those are where the reported profile most often turns out to be wrong.

process.title: Buy one skill for a term
process.description: Agreed in writing with the rate in AED, whether preparation is charged and the reschedule window. One skill for twelve sessions moves a level. Four skills for twelve sessions moves none, which is the commonest way a term of language tutoring produces nothing.

process.title: Review on the same task type
process.description: The same kind of task, at the same phase, six weeks apart: unseen audio at natural speed, or an unprepared speaking prompt, or a text type written cold. Comparison on like material is the only honest review, and if nothing moved we say so and examine whether the skill, the pitch or the hour was wrong.

whyPoints.title: The phase comes first
whyPoints.description: No material is chosen before the registered phase is known, because a level 6 in phase 2 and a level 6 in phase 5 are different achievements requiring different teaching. Material pitched at the wrong phase loses a student within two sessions.

whyPoints.title: Four skills diagnosed separately
whyPoints.description: Listening, reading, speaking and writing are tested individually in the first session, including unseen audio at natural speed and an unprepared prompt. The reported profile is frequently wrong, usually because classroom speech is slower than real speech.

whyPoints.title: Listening sold even though nobody wants it
whyPoints.description: Criterion A is the least requested and most commonly needed purchase in this subject. We will recommend an audio block over conversation practice when the evidence points there, and we will warn you that the first three sessions feel worse before they feel better.

whyPoints.title: Speaking recorded, not discussed
whyPoints.description: A response recorded, heard once and recorded again improves on the second attempt almost every time, and what changes is pace and fillers rather than vocabulary. Three sessions of that beat a term of conversation, because conversation never includes listening back.

whyPoints.title: Arabic expectations set honestly
whyPoints.description: Progress in Arabic as an additional language is slower than in French or Spanish, for reasons of script, diglossia and structure rather than student ability. We say that at the start, and we point families at free daily exposure before selling them hours.

whyPoints.title: A translation line that is not crossed
whyPoints.description: A tutor may teach, drill, rehearse, mark practice work and keep an error log. A tutor does not translate a student's ideas into the target language or write any part of a portfolio submission, because the resulting text demonstrates nothing about the student.

faqs.question: What phase is my child in, and who decides it?
faqs.answer: The school decides, usually through a placement assessment when the student joins the language, and it reviews placement periodically. Phases run from 1 to 6 and describe proficiency rather than year group, so an MYP 5 student can be correctly placed in phase 2 Arabic while an MYP 2 student sits in phase 5 French. If the report does not state the phase, email the language teacher; they will know at once. This is the single most important piece of information in the subject, because the criterion levels are awarded relative to the phase.

faqs.question: Why does my son speak French confidently and still get a 4?
faqs.answer: Most often because speaking is one criterion of four and listening is dragging the grade down. Students get far more practice producing language than following it, and classroom speech is usually slower and more clearly articulated than real speech, so comprehension at natural speed is never properly tested until an assessment. The second possibility is that his fluency is rehearsed: comfortable on prepared topics, stalling on an unseen prompt. Ask for the four criterion levels separately rather than the grade and the cause is usually obvious immediately.

faqs.question: What are the four language acquisition criteria called?
faqs.answer: In the current guide they are listening, reading, speaking and writing, each marked out of eight at the student's phase. Older documentation, still in use on some Abu Dhabi school rubrics, names the same four as comprehending spoken and visual text, comprehending written and visual text, communicating in response to spoken, written and visual text, and using language in spoken and written form. Ask which wording appears on your child's rubric, because the strand descriptions differ in emphasis and a tutor working from the wrong version will practise the wrong things.

faqs.question: Is MYP language acquisition the same as GCSE French or Spanish?
faqs.answer: No, and the differences matter for tutoring. A GCSE course has a published syllabus, defined vocabulary lists, tiers and an external examination at the end. MYP language acquisition has phases rather than tiers, no prescribed vocabulary list, and assessment against four criteria on tasks the school writes, with an externally moderated portfolio available in MYP 5 where a school enters candidates. So a tutor cannot work from a syllabus checklist and past papers. They work from the phase descriptors and your school's own tasks instead.

faqs.question: How is listening assessed, and how do we practise it at home?
faqs.answer: Through spoken and visual material, which includes audio, video and images with on-screen text, with inference from what is heard and seen forming part of the mark. Practice that works is short and fast: thirty to ninety seconds of audio at full natural speed, listened to three times with the questions narrowing each time, never slowed down. Occasional transcription of ten seconds reveals whether the problem is vocabulary or hearing where words divide, which changes the fix completely. Expect it to feel worse for three weeks before it starts improving.

faqs.question: What is the difference between comprehension and inference in reading?
faqs.answer: Comprehension is what the text says; inference is what it implies and how you know. Most students in this emirate handle the first comfortably and avoid the second, so when a task asks about tone, attitude or implication they restate the literal content instead. From phase 3 upwards inference is explicitly part of what is marked. The teachable habit is three questions asked of every text until they become automatic: what is stated, what is implied, and what in the wording tells you so. Three to six sessions usually makes it reliable.

faqs.question: How should my daughter prepare for a speaking assessment?
faqs.answer: By rehearsing unpredictability rather than answers. Classroom speaking is often prepared, while assessment uses unseen prompts and follow-up questions, so fluency on known topics transfers poorly. Record a response to an unseen prompt, listen to it once, and record again. The second attempt is better almost every time, and what improves is pace, filler words and sentences abandoned halfway through, not vocabulary. Three sessions of that changes how a student sounds more than a term of conversation practice, because conversation practice rarely includes hearing yourself back.

faqs.question: What text types does the writing criterion expect?
faqs.answer: It depends on the phase, and the range widens as the phase rises: emails, letters, diary entries, blog posts, brochures, articles, reviews and speeches all appear. Each has conventions of layout, opening, register and closing, and a student who writes an essay when a letter was set has lost marks before the language is assessed. Students ignore text type because nobody has told them it is marked. One sheet listing the conventions for each type, consulted before writing, fixes a surprising proportion of lost criterion D marks in a single session.

faqs.question: Does Arabic as an additional language follow the same MYP criteria?
faqs.answer: Yes, the same four criteria and the same phase system apply. What differs is the rate of progress, and families should expect it to be slower than French or Spanish for three structural reasons: the script is a separate skill so reading and writing lag speaking by about a phase, Standard Arabic differs from the spoken dialect heard around the city, and sentence structure requires real reconstruction rather than word substitution. Arabic is also required in UAE private schools alongside the licensed curriculum, so it is not an optional subject to drop.

faqs.question: Can my child move up a phase during the year?
faqs.answer: The school can move a student, and it does happen, but it is less common than families hope. A phase represents a substantial expansion of range, so moving between phases usually takes a year or more of work, while moving a criterion level within a phase is a term. Expecting a phase change in a term converts normal progress into disappointment. The realistic target for a term of tutoring is one criterion level on one skill, demonstrated on the same kind of task six weeks apart, and that is what we would agree in writing at the start.

faqs.question: Is there an examination in MYP 5 language acquisition?
faqs.answer: Where a school enters candidates for the IB's external assessment, language acquisition is submitted as a portfolio of work rather than sat as an on-screen examination, judged against the standard of the phase the student is registered in. Whether your school enters candidates at all is a school decision, so ask the MYP coordinator rather than assuming. Where it applies, consistency across the year matters more than a single performance, and the text types produced during the year are candidates for submission rather than only practice.

faqs.question: How many sessions does it take to move a criterion level?
faqs.answer: It varies by skill. Reading inference and speaking fluency usually move in three to six sessions, because both respond quickly to a changed habit. Listening and writing take four to eight: listening because comprehension at natural speed has to be built, and writing because accuracy problems are repetitive and need a term of correction to become visible to the student. Moving all four at once in one term is not realistic. Buying one skill for twelve sessions moves a level; spreading twelve sessions across four skills reliably moves nothing.

faqs.question: Should we switch my child's language in MYP 4?
faqs.answer: Rarely, and only with the school's advice. Switching resets a student to phase 1 in a new language, discarding years of accumulated range at exactly the point where the Diploma decision is approaching. The cases where it makes sense are a student stuck in phase 1 after several years with no engagement, or a move to a school that does not offer the original language. If the motivation is that the current language feels hard, the better intervention is usually a listening or accuracy block, because difficulty at phase 3 is normal rather than a signal to leave.

faqs.question: Does language acquisition count towards UAE Ministry of Education equivalency?
faqs.answer: For the British track, the published requirement is five accredited subjects at GCSE or IGCSE with a grade of no less than E or grade 3, and Arabic and Islamic education are specifically not included among those five, plus one Advanced Level subject at E or two Advanced Subsidiary subjects at E. One ranking competitor publishes a six-subject figure, which is wrong. For IB students we will not publish a points threshold because no such figure has been read on the Ministry's own pages. Equivalency is the authority's process, not something a tutor performs, and no part of it requires tutoring.

faqs.question: What can one language session realistically fix?
faqs.answer: A small number of specific things. It can establish the real profile across all four skills, which frequently contradicts the report. It can set up an error log and a text-type sheet, both of which keep paying out afterwards. It can run one recorded speaking cycle, where improvement is audible within the hour. Or it can diagnose whether a listening problem is vocabulary or sound discrimination, which changes the whole approach. What one session cannot do is move a level or change a phase; those take a term and a year respectively.

faqs.question: Are language lessons held at our Abu Dhabi address or online?
faqs.answer: Online. IB Gram does not offer home visits in Abu Dhabi, and visiting tutors are a service we provide only in India. Lessons are one to one, live over video, in Gulf Standard Time. Language teaching loses least of all subjects in this format and arguably gains: audio and video play at full quality through the same channel, speaking practice is recorded and played back inside the session, and your child is matched with a tutor who teaches that language at that phase rather than with whoever teaches it nearby.

abu-dhabi/ib-myp-language-acquisition-tu.closingHeading: Two questions to the language teacher, then one session
abu-dhabi/ib-myp-language-acquisition-tu.closingBody: Before anything is booked, send two questions to your child's language teacher: which phase is my child registered in, and which version of the criterion rubric does the school use? Then ask for the four criterion levels separately rather than the grade. With those answers a specialist can pitch material correctly and test all four skills in one fifty-minute session at no charge, including unseen audio at natural speed and an unprepared speaking prompt. You will finish with a real profile, one named target skill, and an honest estimate of how long a level takes.

abu-dhabi/ib-myp-language-and-literature.tutorsIntro: These tutors teach MYP language and literature: the course taken by students working in the language of instruction at a near-native level. Each marks practice essays against the published criterion strands, annotates drafts with questions rather than corrections, and keeps both versions so the change can be read side by side.

intro.heading: What the record looks like after six weeks of essay work
paragraphs: Writing tuition is the easiest kind to buy on faith and the hardest to verify, because every parent can tell that an essay reads better and almost nobody can tell whether the student is now able to write it unaided. MYP language and literature gives you a way out of that, because the assessment model names four criteria and their strands, and a strand is a specific enough thing to test twice. So the arrangement here is built on comparison: the same text analysed in week one and again in week six, under the same conditions, with both pieces kept.

The four criteria are worth stating plainly, because most Abu Dhabi families have never been told what they are. Criterion A is analysing: the content, context, language, structure, technique and style of a text, the effects of the writer's choices on an audience, opinions justified with examples and terminology, and similarities and differences across texts. Criterion B is organizing: structures that serve the intention, ideas organised coherently, and referencing and formatting used appropriately. Criterion C is producing text: thought, imagination and sensitivity, stylistic choices made with awareness of their impact, and relevant details selected. Criterion D is using language: varied vocabulary and sentence structures, register and style suited to the task, correct grammar, syntax, punctuation and spelling, and clear pronunciation in oral work.

Each is marked out of eight by your child's own teacher, and the four combine into the single 1-7 grade on the report. That combination is where the information disappears. A student at 6 on criterion A and 3 on criterion D is a sharp reader who makes constant grammatical errors. A student at 3 on criterion A and 6 on criterion D writes elegantly about nothing in particular. Both arrive home with a 4 or a 5, and both are routinely sold the same essay-writing course, which will work for neither.

The evidence that settles it is a redraft history. A single improved essay proves that a tutor can improve an essay. Three successive first drafts, each stronger than the last, on three different texts, prove something about the student. That distinction is the whole basis of the arrangement described here, and it is why drafts are kept rather than discarded once the final version has gone in. Parents end a term with a folder they can read rather than a feeling they have to trust.

All of it is delivered one to one, live over video, in Gulf Standard Time. IB Gram does not offer home visits in Abu Dhabi; visiting tutors are a service we run only in India. For essay work the format is well matched: a draft sits on a shared screen with the tutor's questions in the margin, the student answers them in the document while the tutor watches, and every version is saved automatically rather than handed back on paper and lost in a school bag.

abu-dhabi/ib-myp-language-and-literature.programmesIntro: Reading and writing are assessed differently at each stage of the IB continuum, and the skills that carry forward are narrower than most families expect. Analysis carries forward completely. Content does not carry forward at all.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Language and literature is the course for students working in the language of instruction at a near-native level, usually English in Abu Dhabi international schools and Arabic where a school offers Arabic as a first language. Texts are chosen by the school. Assessment is against criteria A to D on tasks the school writes, with an optional on-screen examination in MYP 5.
programmes.countryNote: Abu Dhabi schools licensed by ADEK report criterion levels directly, and language and literature produces the most puzzling reports of any subject because strong writers can score in the middle. ADEK inspects these schools and publishes ratings, which gives a second reference: where the department is rated well and a student sits at a 4, the gap is usually one specific strand rather than general ability.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Becomes language A, as literature or as language and literature, at Standard or Higher Level, with external papers, oral assessment and a written task. The analytical demand rises and the support falls away: students are expected to analyse unseen passages under timed conditions and to sustain comparison across works.
programmes.countryNote: For Abu Dhabi students continuing into the Diploma at the same school, the MYP criterion A record is the single best predictor of difficulty. Unseen passage analysis under time is close to what criterion A asks for, minus the preparation. Students who built that habit in MYP 4 and 5 arrive able to do it; students who relied on knowing the text well in advance find the first Diploma term unpleasant, and the Extended Essay lands on top.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: Language taught across transdisciplinary units, with no criterion grading. Children read widely, respond to texts and write in several forms. There is no criterion level to baseline, so there is nothing for an evidence-led tutoring arrangement to measure.
programmes.countryNote: The transferable preparation before MYP 1 in a continuum school is reading volume and talking about how a book works rather than only what happens in it. A child who can say why a writer began a chapter in a particular place is already doing the first strand of criterion A. That is free, and we would rather recommend it than sell essay tutoring to a nine-year-old.

abu-dhabi/ib-myp-language-and-literature.subjectsIntro: Language and literature sits next to several courses that parents in this emirate regularly confuse with it, and alongside subjects whose levels it directly affects. These are the ones that come up when an essay problem is actually something else.

subjects.name: Language and literature (English)
subjects.description: For students working in the language of instruction at a near-native level. Marked on analysing, organizing, producing text and using language. Levels are lost most often on criterion A, where analysis slides into retelling the plot.

subjects.name: Language and literature (Arabic as a first language)
subjects.description: The same four criteria applied to Arabic texts, taught in Arabic. Required as a first language for Arab students in UAE private schools, and distinct from the MYP language acquisition course that non-Arab students take.

subjects.name: Language acquisition
subjects.description: The course for students learning an additional language, assessed on listening, reading, speaking and writing rather than on literary analysis. Choosing between this and language and literature is a school placement decision, not a parental one.

subjects.name: Individuals and societies
subjects.description: Investigation, source evaluation and argument. Booked alongside language and literature more than any other subject, because a student who cannot structure a paragraph loses levels in both, and fixing the structure once fixes both.

subjects.name: Interdisciplinary units
subjects.description: Separately assessed units pairing language and literature with another group, often individuals and societies in this emirate. They carry their own criteria and grade, and the language half tends to be marked more strictly than students expect.

subjects.name: Design
subjects.description: Produces a process journal, which is the closest thing in the MYP to the draft history this page argues for. Students who keep one well transfer the habit to essay work, where successive drafts become the record of improvement.

subjects.name: Arts
subjects.description: Investigating, developing, creating and evaluating. Its evaluation strand asks for the same reflective writing that criterion C in language and literature rewards, so students often improve both at once without noticing.

subjects.name: Sciences
subjects.description: Relevant because criterion D in sciences requires a written discussion of impacts, and students who cannot build a paragraph lose science levels for writing reasons. Essay structure taught here pays out in a subject nobody associates with writing.

subjects.name: Personal project
subjects.description: A substantial independent piece with its own criteria and a written report. The writing demands are real, and the authorship rules are strict: a supervisor signs off on authenticity, so the report must be the student's own work entirely.

subjects.name: Islamic education and social studies
subjects.description: Federally required alongside the licensed curriculum, with their own written tasks in their own languages of instruction. They occupy evenings, which is the practical reason an ambitious essay-tutoring schedule in Abu Dhabi tends to collapse by week four.

regions.name: Saadiyat Island

sections.heading: The same text, analysed twice, six weeks apart
paragraphs: The hardest question in writing tuition is whether the student has improved or whether the tutor has. One heavily supported essay answers nothing. The measure that does answer it is a repeat under identical conditions: the same passage, the same time limit, no notes, no help, in week one and again in week six. Both pieces are kept, and the difference between them is the result.

This works because criterion A is a skill rather than a body of knowledge. A student who can analyse the structure of a passage, identify the effect of a writer's choices and justify an opinion with an example and a term can do that on any passage, which means improvement shows up on a repeat rather than on a new topic. It also exposes the opposite case honestly. A student whose second attempt is no stronger has not learned the skill, whatever happened in the sessions in between, and six weeks is early enough to change course.

Choosing the passage matters. It should be something the school is not assessing, long enough to have structure, and unfamiliar at the start. A short non-literary text often works better than an extract from a novel, because it removes the advantage of having read the book. The conditions should be written down: the time limit, whether a dictionary is allowed, whether the student may plan on paper. Parents can run the repeat themselves if they prefer, which some do, and it makes the comparison harder to argue with.

The second part of the record is the draft sequence. For each assessed task, the first draft, the annotated version and the student's rewrite are all kept. Over a term that produces three or four sequences, and the useful pattern is in the first drafts rather than the final ones. If the week-twelve first draft is already doing what the week-two annotated version had to be told to do, the teaching has landed. If the first drafts are identical and only the final versions improve, something else has been happening.

sections.heading: Where analysis stops and retelling begins
paragraphs: The most common reason a well-written essay scores a 4 in this subject is that it describes the text instead of analysing it. The student explains what happens, in order, accurately and fluently, and then states that this is effective. Criterion A asks for something different: analysis of content, context, language, structure, technique and style, and analysis of the effects of the creator's choices on an audience. The word doing the work is choices.

The practical distinction is easy to teach and hard to habituate. Retelling says what is in the text. Analysis says what the writer did and what it does to a reader. 'The narrator describes the room in detail' is retelling. 'The narrator catalogues the room's objects without naming a single person, which delays the reader's sense that anyone lives there' is analysis, because it identifies a choice and names an effect. Students can usually produce the second sentence when asked directly, and revert to the first when writing at length, which is why the fix is repetition on short passages rather than discussion on long ones.

The third strand of criterion A compounds the problem: opinions must be justified using examples, explanations and terminology. Students supply the opinion and omit one of the three, most often the explanation, so the essay becomes a list of quotations with labels attached. Teaching the three-part move, which is claim, evidence, then the explanation of how the evidence supports the claim, is worth a level on its own and takes two or three sessions of deliberately short paragraphs.

The fourth strand asks for evaluation of similarities and differences by connecting features across and within genres and texts. This is where MYP 4 and 5 students lose most heavily, because comparison is treated as two essays stapled together. A comparative paragraph has to move between texts within itself, and the organising idea must be a feature rather than a text. That reorganisation is a criterion B skill as much as a criterion A one, which is why the two are usually taught in the same term.

sections.heading: Criterion B: the essay that has good ideas and no shape
paragraphs: Criterion B, organizing, has three strands: employing organisational structures that serve the context and intention, organising opinions and ideas in a sustained, coherent and logical manner, and using referencing and formatting tools to create a presentation style suitable to the task. It is the criterion that most rewards planning and the one students are most confident they do not need.

The failure is recognisable at a glance. Paragraphs that each contain two or three ideas, in the order the student thought of them. An introduction that announces the topic without stating a position. A conclusion that repeats the introduction in different words. Transitions that signal sequence rather than logic, so the essay moves from one point to the next without any point following from the one before. None of that is a writing-quality problem, which is why students who write attractive sentences are so often surprised by a criterion B level of 3.

The repair is structural and quick, because it happens before the writing. One idea per paragraph, written as a single sentence in a plan. The plan read back in order to check that the sequence argues something rather than lists it. A position stated in the opening. A conclusion that answers rather than restates. Five sessions of planning essays without writing them moves criterion B more than twenty sessions of writing essays without planning them, and students resent it for about two weeks before they notice their drafts taking half the time.

The third strand, referencing and formatting, is the cheap part. Quotations punctuated and attributed consistently, a format that matches what the task asked for, and a presentation style suited to the intention. A student who writes an essay when a speech was set has lost a strand before the content is read. Reading the task sheet for the required form takes thirty seconds and is skipped routinely.
