faqs.question: How is MYP Spanish actually graded in an Abu Dhabi school?
faqs.answer: Against four published criteria, each worth 8 marks: comprehending spoken and visual text, comprehending written and visual text, communicating in response to text, and using language in spoken and written form. The school marks tasks against descriptor bands for your child's phase, then converts the profile into a subject grade from 1 to 7 using published boundaries. Ask for the criterion breakdown rather than the grade, because a profile of 7, 4, 6, 4 and a flat profile of 5, 5, 5, 5 look similar on a report and need completely different work. The breakdown is the document that tells you what to do.

faqs.question: Why does my child speak Spanish confidently but still score a 5?
faqs.answer: Because confidence is rewarded under two criteria and penalised by neither, while the grade is an average across four. A fluent speaker typically scores well on criterion A, where context carries them, and on criterion C, where they have something to say. The grade then sits in the middle because criterion B asks them to infer purpose and audience from text they have never seen, and criterion D asks for accuracy under time pressure. Both of those are trainable, by different methods: a reading routine for B, and short corrected production with an error log for D.

faqs.question: Which Spanish grammar errors cost the most marks at MYP level?
faqs.answer: Eight patterns account for most criterion D loss. Ser against estar, chosen by instinct because English merges them. Preterite against imperfect, where students narrate in a single tense. Subjunctive triggers recognised too late rather than forms unknown. Gender and number agreement degrading after the first two sentences. Por and para learned as a list rather than a principle. False friends with English. Written accents that change a tense or a meaning. And register, including the tú and usted decision. An error log kept for three weeks will usually show that only two of the eight are actually costing your child marks.

faqs.question: How is the Spanish oral task marked, and does speaking fast help?
faqs.answer: Speaking fast does not help and often hurts. The spoken task is assessed under criteria C and D, which reward addressing the stimulus and the stated purpose, and using accurate language in an appropriate register. A student who talks quickly, fills pauses in English and talks around the prompt will score below a slower student who answers it, repairs their own errors in Spanish and holds the register. The productive method is to record the student, mark the recording against the descriptor, and annotate a transcript so they can see the loss points instead of being told about them.

faqs.question: What goes into a Language Acquisition ePortfolio for Spanish?
faqs.answer: Where a school enters MYP eAssessment, Language Acquisition is evidenced through a portfolio of the student's own work produced over months rather than a single sat paper. The components a school enters vary and not every Abu Dhabi school takes that route, so confirm with the MYP coordinator which route your child is on before planning around it. Where it applies, support looks like a structured habit of drafting, criterion-referenced feedback and revision across the year. It rewards consistency and record-keeping, and it punishes students who produce strong single pieces and keep no account of their process.

faqs.question: Does a missing accent in Spanish writing actually lose marks?
faqs.answer: It can, because in Spanish an accent is not decoration. It distinguishes tenses and meanings, so a missing or misplaced mark can change what the sentence says rather than merely how it looks. Under criterion D, which assesses accuracy and range, repeated accent errors read as a control problem. The practical fix is narrow and quick: a student only needs the small set of contrasts that recur in their own writing, found from an error log rather than from a textbook list. Most students fix this in two or three weeks once someone has shown them which pairs matter for them.

faqs.question: Can my child use a translation app for Spanish homework?
faqs.answer: The rule we teach is that a tool may check something the student has already produced, never produce it for them. Looking up a word or confirming a gender on a finished sentence is reasonable. Typing an English paragraph in and copying out the Spanish is not: the student learns nothing, the register is usually wrong for the task, and the accuracy will be inconsistent with their classwork in a way teachers notice. Work submitted for assessment must be the student's own, and the consequence of misrepresenting a machine's output as their own falls on the student.

faqs.question: My child started Spanish in MYP 3 - which phase should they be in?
faqs.answer: A genuine beginner starting in MYP 3 would normally be placed in Phase 1 or 2, working on familiar topics with heavy support, and would progress towards Phase 3 by the end of MYP 4 with consistent study. The risk in a late start is placement into a continuer group for timetabling reasons rather than for level, which produces permanent criterion D scores of 3 or 4 and a student who concludes they are bad at languages. Ask the MYP coordinator which phase is on record and which descriptors are being used, then compare that against what your child can do with an unfamiliar short text.

faqs.question: Is Phase 3 Spanish at the end of MYP 5 enough for Diploma Spanish B?
faqs.answer: Phase 3 at the end of MYP 5 makes Spanish B at SL realistic and HL difficult. Phase 4 makes SL secure and HL achievable with work. Phase 5 makes HL realistic. The decision that matters is taken earlier than families expect, because phase progression is cumulative: the trajectory through MYP 3 and 4 is what determines where a student finishes. A student who has studied Spanish for years is also generally ineligible for ab initio, which is designed for near-beginners, so parking below level in MYP 4 narrows rather than preserves the options.

faqs.question: What exactly does criterion D measure in spoken Spanish?
faqs.answer: Accuracy, range and register in speech - whether the grammar holds up in real time, whether the vocabulary reaches beyond the rehearsed, and whether the formality suits the task and the audience. It is not a measure of volume or speed. The commonest losses are tense control slipping once the student is improvising, agreement errors appearing after the first few sentences, English fillers breaking the register, and a tú or usted choice that does not match the situation described in the prompt. All four are visible on a recording and none of them are visible in a conversation nobody recorded.

faqs.question: The Spanish report says 5 - what is missing for a 7?
faqs.answer: Almost always two things, and they are rarely vocabulary. The first is inference under criterion B: the ability to read a text never seen before and state what it wants the reader to think or do, with the licensing phrase identified. The second is accuracy under time pressure under criterion D, where the gap between what a student knows and what they produce in twenty minutes is widest. Ask for the criterion breakdown and look at which two numbers are lowest. A two-mark movement on each of two criteria is usually what separates a 5 from a 6 or 7.

faqs.question: Do Abu Dhabi schools teach Spanish from Spain or from Latin America?
faqs.answer: Both are taught and both are acceptable in assessment - the descriptors assess comprehension, communication and accurate use of language, not a single national variety. What matters is consistency within a piece of work, because mixing varieties mid-paragraph reads as a control problem under criterion D. It is worth asking your child's department which variety its materials use, so a tutor works with the same one and the student is not corrected in two directions at once. Vocabulary differences are the visible part; the pronoun and past-tense usage differences matter more for writing.

faqs.question: Can a tutor mark Spanish work the same way my child's department does?
faqs.answer: Where the tutor works from the published criteria and the phase descriptors the school is using, yes - and that is the point of asking which phase is on record before anything else. What a tutor cannot do is predict a school's internal grade boundaries, which schools set for their own tasks. What they can do is say which descriptor band a piece of work sits in, name the specific feature keeping it there, and mark the next piece the same way so movement is visible. That consistency is more useful to a student than a number.

faqs.question: Is it too late to fix Spanish accuracy in the final MYP year?
faqs.answer: Accuracy is the most improvable part of the subject late on, which makes MYP 5 a better year for criterion D work than for criterion B work. Short corrected production several times a week, with an error log, moves tense control and agreement within a term because those are habits rather than knowledge gaps. Inference under criterion B improves more slowly and is better started in MYP 3 or 4. The constraint in MYP 5 is the calendar rather than the subject: the Personal Project runs in the same year and competes for the same evenings, so the plan has to be realistic about hours.

faqs.question: Does a Spanish-speaking parent at home help or hurt the grade?
faqs.answer: It helps criteria A and C and can quietly damage criterion D. Conversation and listening practice with a fluent speaker at home is valuable and entirely legitimate - it builds exactly the comprehension and confidence the first two criteria reward. Editing drafts is the problem: writing corrected by a fluent adult produces work the student cannot reproduce under timed conditions, which inflates the apparent level, hides the real one and leaves the student unprepared. Keep the two uses apart, and a Spanish-speaking household is one of the strongest assets a MYP language student can have.

Send a recent marked Spanish task and the last criterion profile, and the free trial lesson - one lesson, one student, no card details, nothing payable - will produce a written phase judgement, one named criterion to target first, and a date by which movement should be visible in marked work. Sessions run one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time, scheduled around the Abu Dhabi school run, with short written or recorded work marked between them.

abu-dhabi/ib-myp-standard-mathematics-tu.tutorsIntro: The tutors below teach the standard mathematics route as a course in its own right rather than as a lighter version of something else. That means the full standard syllabus, criterion-marked task technique, and an honest view of which Diploma mathematics courses follow from it. Tell us the year and the four criterion levels from the last report.

intro.heading: Standard is a route, not a ranking
paragraphs: At the start of MYP 4, mathematics in an IB school divides. Half a year group continues on what the programme calls standard mathematics and the other half moves onto extended. Many Abu Dhabi families read that split as setting, hear the word standard, and conclude their child has been placed in the lower group. That reading causes a specific and avoidable kind of damage: a student who believes they are in the weak set stops trying to reach the top descriptor bands, and a 7 that was available quietly becomes a 5.

The accurate reading is different. Standard mathematics covers the core of the MYP mathematics framework and is assessed against exactly the same four criteria as extended, each scored one to eight, with the same maximum total and the same grade scale running to 7. Extended adds breadth and algebraic depth on top of the core; it does not replace it with harder versions of the same ideas. A student on standard who understands proportional reasoning deeply and can justify a general rule is doing better mathematics than a student on extended who has memorised the cosine rule and cannot say when it applies.

What follows from that is the point of this page. If standard is a route rather than a ranking, then tutoring on it should look like teaching a course properly rather than like remediation. The work is to secure the standard syllabus, raise the criterion levels that are low, and get the student to the top descriptor bands that the standard route genuinely offers. Nothing about that requires pretending the extended content is coming. It requires knowing the standard syllabus precisely and knowing where its own difficulty sits.

There is a second honest conversation, and it is about the Diploma. The route a student finishes MYP on shapes which of the four Diploma mathematics courses are comfortable two years later. Applications and Interpretation at both levels, and Analysis and Approaches at Standard Level, are reachable from the standard route without heroics. Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level is a real stretch from it, and families whose child is aiming at engineering or physics should know that in MYP 4 rather than in DP1. Saying so is not an argument for moving routes. It is an argument for making the choice with the information.

A note on how any of this is delivered. IB Gram's tutoring for UAE families is one-to-one and online, over live video on Gulf Standard Time. IB Gram does not offer home visits in the UAE; home visits are a service we run only in India. For mathematics the online format is a genuine advantage, because a shared digital writing surface shows a student's working line by line, keeps a record of it, and lets a graph be redrawn in seconds. Matching without a driving radius also means a family in Al Shamkha or Al Samha chooses from the same tutors as a family on Saadiyat Island.

abu-dhabi/ib-myp-standard-mathematics-tu.programmesIntro: The standard route sits inside a longer sequence, and its job is to leave a student able to do the next thing. The programmes below are described by what they expect a student to arrive already able to do, which is the test that matters when choosing a route.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Mathematics runs as a single course through MYP 1 to 3 and then divides into standard and extended for MYP 4 and 5. Both routes are assessed against knowing and understanding, investigating patterns, communicating, and applying mathematics in real-life contexts, each scored one to eight. Both can reach a subject grade of 7. The optional on-screen examination in the final year is available on either route.
programmes.countryNote: Abu Dhabi MYP cohorts span long-established island schools and fast-growing ones along the Khalifa City, Al Raha and Yas corridor. In several newer schools the route decision is taken by the mathematics department on the basis of MYP 3 criterion levels, with limited scope to appeal, which makes the MYP 3 year quietly decisive for a family with a Diploma plan in mind.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Four mathematics options: Analysis and Approaches or Applications and Interpretation, each at Standard or Higher Level. Each carries a twenty-mark exploration worth about a fifth of the subject grade. The content assumption at entry is not the same across the four, which is the whole reason the MYP route matters.
programmes.countryNote: Abu Dhabi schools generally offer at least three of the four combinations, and Applications and Interpretation has grown as a sensible destination for students from the standard route who still want substantial mathematics. Where a school offers only two combinations, the route decision in MYP 4 constrains the Diploma choice more tightly than the family expects.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: Mathematics is taught through inquiry with no criterion levels. What it leaves behind is number sense: a student who is fluent with fractions, place value and multiplicative reasoning arrives in MYP 1 able to spend attention on the mathematics rather than on the arithmetic underneath it.
programmes.countryNote: Abu Dhabi families often transfer between systems during the primary years, and a child arriving into MYP 1 from a curriculum that emphasised procedure over reasoning meets criterion B for the first time with no preparation for it. That is the gap that shows up again at the route decision three years later.

programmes.name: Cambridge and Pearson IGCSE
programmes.description: The parallel the standard route most resembles in level, though not in assessment style. Cambridge mathematics 0580 is tiered Core and Extended; Pearson 4MA1 is tiered Foundation and Higher. Both are examined by written papers with no criterion marking and no investigation component, which is the real difference a transferring student feels.
programmes.countryNote: Because Abu Dhabi has large British-curriculum cohorts alongside IB ones, families compare the two constantly. The practical point is that an IGCSE Higher or Extended tier student transferring into MYP standard will find the content familiar and the criterion B expectations entirely new.

abu-dhabi/ib-myp-standard-mathematics-tu.subjectsIntro: The grid below is the standard mathematics syllabus as a student meets it, with the difficulty that actually sits inside each strand. Where extended goes further, that is noted, so the shape of the route is visible rather than implied.

subjects.name: Number and the four operations in context
subjects.description: Integers, fractions, decimals, percentages and the discipline of choosing an operation from a described situation. The difficulty here is not calculation but selection: a student who can divide perfectly often cannot tell from a worded context that division is what the situation wants.

subjects.name: Ratio, proportion and rates
subjects.description: The strand that quietly determines a standard-route grade. Direct and inverse proportion, scale, unit rates and percentage change recur in geometry, in statistics and in every real-life application task, so a weakness here is paid for four times over.

subjects.name: Algebraic expressions and linear equations
subjects.description: Simplifying, substituting, expanding single brackets, solving linear and simultaneous equations. Standard treats quadratic work lightly where extended treats it as central. The standard-route difficulty is forming an equation from words rather than solving one that is given.

subjects.name: Sequences and general rules
subjects.description: Linear and simple non-linear sequences, expressed as a general rule in terms of position. This is where the standard route's criterion B tasks live, and where a student can reach the top descriptor band without any extended content at all, provided they justify rather than describe.

subjects.name: Coordinate geometry and straight-line graphs
subjects.description: Plotting, gradient, intercepts and interpreting a line in context. Standard asks what the gradient means in the situation modelled; extended goes on into transformations and non-linear function families. Reading a gradient as a rate is the transferable skill.

subjects.name: Geometry: angles, polygons and reasoning
subjects.description: Angle facts, properties of shapes, similarity and congruence, with reasons stated. The assessment is the reasoning rather than the answer, and standard-route students lose levels on criterion C by producing the right number with no justification attached.

subjects.name: Mensuration: perimeter, area, surface area and volume
subjects.description: Compound shapes, prisms, cylinders and conversion between units. Reliably taught and reliably examined, and one of the few strands where sustained practice does genuinely move criterion A levels quickly.

subjects.name: Right-angled trigonometry and Pythagoras
subjects.levels: Standard route · extended adds sine and cosine rules
subjects.description: Standard covers right-angled triangles thoroughly and stops there. Extended continues into non-right-angled cases. A standard-route student who is secure on right angles and on labelling has everything the route asks for.

subjects.name: Statistics: collecting, representing, interpreting
subjects.description: Choosing a representation, calculating measures of centre and spread, and saying what a dataset does and does not support. Criterion D tasks lean on this heavily, and the missing step is almost always the interpretive sentence rather than the calculation.

subjects.name: Probability of single and combined events
subjects.levels: Standard route · extended adds conditional cases
subjects.description: Sample spaces, tree diagrams and two-way tables, with independent and mutually exclusive events. Standard stops before conditional probability. Students lose marks by computing correctly and then stating a conclusion the probability does not support.

subjects.name: Real-life modelling tasks
subjects.description: Taking a situation, choosing a mathematical model, applying it and then evaluating how well it fits. The top descriptor band requires the evaluation, and it is the single most commonly omitted sentence in standard-route work across every school.

subjects.name: On-screen examination technique
subjects.description: Reading a scenario on screen, working on paper, and entering a response in an acceptable form. Standard-route candidates sit a paper pitched at the standard syllabus, so the technique matters more than extra content: lost time, not lost knowledge, is the usual cost.

abu-dhabi/ib-myp-standard-mathematics-tu.regionsIntro: What differs between Abu Dhabi communities on this page is not price but circumstance: how a school handles the route decision, how often families transfer between curricula, and how much of the week is already committed before an evening session can happen.

regions.name: Saadiyat Island
regions.note: Established schools with large year groups, so the route decision is usually made on several terms of criterion evidence rather than one test. Students here often have heavy co-curricular commitments, so the realistic session is late evening or weekend rather than straight after school.

regions.name: Al Reem Island
regions.note: A high proportion of mid-year arrivals from other systems, which is the group most likely to be placed on standard on arrival and most likely to be misread as struggling. A diagnostic across all four criteria is worth more here than extra practice on whatever the class is currently doing.

regions.name: Khalifa City
regions.note: Long bus journeys from island schools mean a student is often home after half past four and tired. For standard-route work that argues for shorter, more frequent sessions on specific criteria rather than a single long weekly hour that ends in diminishing returns.

regions.name: Al Raha Beach and Al Raha Gardens
regions.note: Dense MYP population feeding a handful of schools, so route decisions and reporting rounds happen simultaneously across many households. Families here often compare their child's placement with a neighbour's, which is where the standard-is-the-lower-set misreading spreads fastest.

regions.name: Al Bateen and Al Khalidiyah
regions.note: Mixed-curriculum streets where a standard-route MYP student has friends sitting IGCSE Higher tier. The comparison is unhelpful because the assessment styles differ, and explaining that difference to the student is sometimes the most useful thing a first session does.

regions.name: Yas Island and West Yas
regions.note: Newer cohorts where the mathematics department may be small and the route decision correspondingly blunt. A standard placement here is more likely to be provisional than permanent, so securing the core and documenting criterion levels is the practical route to a review.

regions.name: Mohammed Bin Zayed City and Shakhbout City
regions.note: Large mainland households with several children at different stages. Standard-route work benefits from a predictable slot that does not depend on a car being free, which is the ordinary constraint in a household running three school runs.

regions.name: Al Shamkha, Al Falah and Al Reef
regions.note: Thin local supply of tutors who have marked MYP criterion tasks, as opposed to tutors who can teach the content. Since the standard route's difficulty sits in criterion B and D technique rather than in the content, that distinction matters more here than anywhere.

schoolClusters.note: Large, long-running MYP mathematics departments where standard and extended both carry full classes and the route decision is evidence-based. Students we support attend schools in this cluster; ADEK publishes the licensing and inspection record for each one.

abu-dhabi/ib-myp-standard-mathematics-tu.modesIntro: Standard-route support divides by what is actually wrong, and the four shapes below are genuinely different pieces of teaching rather than different durations of the same one.

modes.title: Securing the core
modes.description: For a student whose criterion A levels are low because earlier content never settled. The work is ratio, proportion, algebraic notation and mensuration, taught until they are automatic. This is the most productive thing available on the standard route, because almost every lost level elsewhere traces back to an unsecured core topic rather than to the topic being assessed.
bullets: Diagnostic across number, ratio, algebra and mensuration first
Short, frequent practice with marking at the start of each session
Targets written as criterion levels, not as topic ticks
Finishes when a mixed task is answered without arithmetic leakage

modes.title: Criterion B investigation technique
modes.description: The standard route's top band is reached through justification, not through harder content. Sessions take a sequence or a geometric pattern, require a general rule, and then refuse to accept the rule until the student has verified it and said why it holds. It is slow work and it is the difference between a 5 and a 7 on this route.
bullets: Pattern to general rule to verification to justification, every time
Written in the student's own words, not supplied
Worked on standard-syllabus material only; no extended content needed
Measured by re-marking the same style of task after four sessions

modes.title: Criterion D application and the evaluation sentence
modes.description: The cheapest level on the standard route. Students model a situation competently and then stop, never saying how well the model fits or what it ignores. Teaching that final paragraph takes two or three sessions and moves criterion D immediately, because the mathematics was already there.
bullets: Choosing a model and saying why it suits the situation
Naming the assumptions the model makes
A closing judgement on fit and limitations
Transfers directly into the Diploma exploration two years later

modes.title: Route review preparation
modes.description: For families who believe a standard placement was made on thin evidence and want a review at the end of MYP 4. The work is to secure the standard core, demonstrate criterion B at the upper bands, and close the specific extended topics the school will ask about. It is an honest ask, not a guaranteed outcome, and the school decides.
bullets: Standard core secured and evidenced before anything else
Criterion B at the top bands on standard material
Targeted work on quadratics and trigonometry beyond right angles
A clear statement that the school, not a tutor, makes the decision

sections.heading: What standard mathematics actually is, answered literally
paragraphs: Standard mathematics is the core route of MYP mathematics in years four and five of the programme, running alongside extended mathematics rather than beneath it. It uses the same four assessment criteria, the same one-to-eight level scale, the same thirty-two-point total and the same subject grades one to seven. A student on standard can be awarded a 7. The route determines the breadth of content, not the ceiling of achievement.

The content difference is best described as depth in algebra and reach in a few named topics. Extended carries the full quadratic treatment, non-right-angled trigonometry, function transformations and conditional probability. Standard covers linear algebra thoroughly, right-angled trigonometry thoroughly, single-event and combined probability, and the whole of number, ratio, geometry, mensuration and statistics. Framed that way it is obvious that standard is not a reduced syllabus so much as a differently bounded one.

Why the misreading persists is worth naming, because it affects outcomes. Schools often make the route decision at the end of MYP 3 using criterion levels, and a letter home that says a child has been placed on standard reads to a parent exactly like a setting decision. The student then hears it the same way. From that point, the realistic ceiling in their own mind drops, effort on the top descriptor bands stops, and the self-fulfilling version of the misreading arrives in the next report. A tutor's first job on this route is frequently to undo that, which takes one honest conversation and a task the student succeeds at.
bullets: Same four criteria, same one-to-eight levels, same grade ceiling of 7
Extended adds depth in algebra and reach in four named topics
The route is a content boundary, not an ability label
Undoing the lower-set reading is often the first useful session

sections.heading: The standard syllabus beside extended, strand by strand
paragraphs: Families deciding about routes, or wondering what a standard-route student has not met, are rarely shown the two syllabuses side by side. The comparison below is the practical version: what standard covers, where extended goes further, and what the difference means for a student sitting a criterion-marked task.

Read down the middle column first. Everything there is content a standard-route student is expected to handle at the top descriptor bands, which is the thing most worth remembering. A 7 on standard requires complete security across that column plus genuine justification on criterion B, and that is a demanding combination. It is not reached by drifting.

Read the right-hand column second, and only with a purpose. If your child is heading for Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level, those rows are the gap and it is worth knowing its size. If they are not, those rows are simply other people's syllabus and chasing them steals time from the standard core, which is where the available levels actually are. The commonest wasted tutoring on this route is extended content taught to a student who has not secured ratio. One further use for the comparison is conversational. A standard-route student who has heard from a friend on extended that they are doing the cosine rule often concludes that they are being given less mathematics. Showing them the middle column, and pointing out that criterion B at the top band is available on everything in it, is a more honest answer than reassurance and it changes how the next task gets attempted.

sections.heading: The four criteria read for a standard-route student
paragraphs: A criterion-marked report gives four numbers and no explanation, and the explanation is where the useful information lives. What follows is each criterion described by the step a standard-route student typically does not take, because that step is the whole difference between the level they have and the level above it.

Criterion A rewards applying procedures accurately in both familiar and unfamiliar situations, and the word unfamiliar is doing the work. A student who is fluent on exercises and freezes on a rearranged question is sitting in the middle bands by design, not by accident. Criterion C rewards notation, terminology and a logical line of working, which sounds cosmetic and is not: a solution where line three does not follow from line two is marked down whether or not the final answer is right.

Criterion B is the route's real opportunity. It asks a student to find a pattern, express it as a general rule, verify the rule and justify why it holds. A standard-route student who gets to justification is in the top bands using only standard content. Most do not, because describing the pattern feels like the answer. Criterion D asks for a model, applied and then evaluated, and the evaluation is the sentence nobody writes. Both of those are technique rather than content, which is exactly why a standard-route student has as much access to the top of the scale as anybody. The practical reading of a four-number report, then, is to look for the gap between the highest and the lowest level rather than at the average. A profile of 7, 4, 7, 5 is not a student who is averagely good at mathematics; it is a strong mathematician who has never been taught to justify or evaluate, and the two low numbers are the cheapest to move.

sections.heading: Where standard-route levels are actually lost
paragraphs: Four failure modes account for most of the lost levels on this route, and all four are diagnosable from a single piece of marked work. None of them is about the student being bad at mathematics, which is the diagnosis families fear and the one that is almost never correct.

The first is arithmetic leakage: a correct method undermined by a slip in fractions, negatives or place value. It costs criterion A marks and it compounds, because a wrong intermediate value makes the rest of the solution unverifiable. The second is the word-problem translation gap, where a student who can solve an equation cannot form one from a described situation. That is criterion D as much as criterion A, and it responds to practice on forming rather than solving.

The third is the justification stop, already described, and it is the largest single cause of a capped criterion B. The fourth is presentation that hides thinking: unlabelled diagrams, no units, steps omitted because they felt obvious. Criterion C is explicitly about this, and it is the fastest level on the whole route to recover, because the mathematics is already correct and only the record of it is missing. A student who starts writing units and labelling axes gains a level in a fortnight. Worth adding that none of the four shows up as a topic name on a report, which is why parents so often conclude that the problem is the current unit of work. It is almost never the current unit. A marked task from any point in the year will display the same four signatures, and that is what makes a single piece of marked work worth more to a diagnosis than a term of verbal updates from anyone.
bullets: Arithmetic leakage inside a correct method, costing criterion A
Forming an equation from words, as distinct from solving one
Stopping at the described pattern instead of justifying the rule
Omitted units, labels and steps, which criterion C marks directly

sections.heading: From standard mathematics into the Diploma: which doors stay open
paragraphs: This is the conversation that should happen in MYP 4 and usually happens in DP1. The four Diploma mathematics courses make different assumptions about what a student arrives able to do, and the standard route leaves some of them comfortable and one of them hard.

Applications and Interpretation at Standard Level follows naturally and is a sound destination. Applications and Interpretation at Higher Level is reachable with work, and it is a serious mathematics course rather than a soft option; it carries statistics and modelling that many degree routes genuinely want. Analysis and Approaches at Standard Level is reachable with a bridging effort concentrated on quadratics and function behaviour. Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level is the hard one, because it assumes the algebraic fluency that extended mathematics was building.

What to do with that information depends entirely on the degree, not on pride. If a student is aiming at engineering, physics or certain economics and medicine routes at UAE or overseas universities, Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level is commonly expected and the gap from standard should be planned for deliberately. If they are not, then Applications and Interpretation is not a consolation prize and treating it as one causes families to force a student into a course they will struggle in. The table below states the gap honestly in each direction. One more practical point: Abu Dhabi schools do not all offer all four combinations, and a school running only two will constrain the choice further. Ask the Diploma coordinator which combinations run in practice rather than which appear in the prospectus, because a course that attracts four candidates in a given year sometimes does not run at all, and that is a fact worth having before the MYP 4 route decision is made rather than after.

sections.heading: Arriving on the standard route from another system
paragraphs: Abu Dhabi has a high rate of mid-secondary transfer, and a student arriving into MYP 4 from a British, American, Indian or national-curriculum school is frequently placed on standard simply because there is no criterion evidence to place them anywhere else. That is a reasonable administrative decision and a poor diagnosis, and it is worth separating the two.

What such a student usually has is content. A Year 10 arrival from a British school has met most of the standard syllabus and quite a lot of the extended one. What they have not met is criterion marking: the requirement to justify a general rule, to evaluate a model, and to produce working that a marker can follow as reasoning rather than as arithmetic. That is a technique gap of a few weeks, not a content gap of a year, and recognising which one you are dealing with saves a term.

The transition map below sets out what typically carries over and what has to be built, by origin system. It is the version of this comparison nobody publishes, and it is the most practically useful thing on the page for a family that moved to Abu Dhabi recently. The honest headline is that transferring students are often misplaced downwards and recover the route at the end of MYP 4 once there is evidence, provided somebody has spent the intervening months on criterion technique rather than on content they already knew.

sections.heading: The on-screen examination, read from the standard side
paragraphs: In the final MYP year schools may enter candidates for on-screen examinations, and mathematics is among the subjects available. Entry is a school decision, and plenty of good Abu Dhabi schools do not enter candidates at all, so the first thing to establish is whether this applies to your child before spending anything on it.

Where it does apply, the standard-route paper is pitched at the standard syllabus, which has a useful consequence: the preparation is not about learning more content. It is about handling a scenario-based, on-screen format under time pressure. Students who have practised only on paper lose time rather than marks, and time is the resource the paper is short of. Reading a scenario on screen, working on paper beside it, and then entering a response in a form the interface accepts is a skill with a short learning curve and a real cost if it is met for the first time on the day.

The second feature worth preparing for is that on-screen tasks tend to be context-heavy, which pushes them towards criteria D and B rather than pure criterion A recall. For a standard-route student who has spent the year securing procedures, that is a mismatch worth closing in advance with two or three timed practices. A tutor's useful contribution here is marking those attempts against the criteria rather than against an answer key, and reporting which criterion lost the marks. A final caution about what the component is worth. The MYP certificate matters for some school-to-school transfers and for a school's own internal progression decisions, and it matters very little to a university three years later. Preparing for it is sensible if the school has entered your child. Paying for a long programme of preparation for a component nobody downstream will ask about is not.
bullets: Entry is a school decision; confirm it applies before preparing for it
The standard paper is pitched at the standard syllabus, so no new content is needed
The cost of unfamiliarity is lost time, not lost knowledge
Scenario-heavy tasks lean on criteria B and D rather than recall

sections.heading: What one session fixes, and what it cannot
paragraphs: A page selling tutoring should be clear about the unit of change, because families often expect a session to do work that only a term can do, and then conclude that tutoring does not work. Some things genuinely move in an hour. Others do not move in ten.

In one session you can fix a notation habit, teach the structure of a criterion D evaluation paragraph, correct a persistent misconception about negatives or inverse proportion, and show a student what a justified general rule looks like as opposed to a described pattern. Those are real, visible changes and the next piece of marked work will show them. In two or three sessions you can usually move criterion C by a level, because it is largely habit, and criterion D by a level, because the mathematics was already present.

What one session cannot do is build fluency, which requires repetition spread over weeks; close an arithmetic gap carried from primary school, which takes a bounded block of frequent short practice; or produce the judgement criterion B rewards, which is slow because it is genuinely a skill. Nor can any number of sessions substitute for work between them. A student who does nothing between sessions is buying a weekly demonstration, and the honest thing to say is that it will not move a report. The useful way to set expectations, then, is to agree in advance which of those two categories the goal belongs to. A notation problem has a two-week answer. A criterion B problem has a six-to-eight-session answer and needs work between every one of them. Telling a family which they have bought is the difference between tutoring that gets credited with a result and tutoring that gets quietly blamed for the absence of one.
bullets: One session: a notation habit, a misconception, the shape of an evaluation
Two or three: criterion C and criterion D by a level each
A bounded block: fluency, arithmetic repair, criterion B judgement
No number of sessions replaces practice between them

sections.heading: Honesty, the regulator and the permit
paragraphs: Three things a parent should be able to check before paying anyone, stated here with their sources. First, what a tutor may do with assessed work. MYP tasks and the Personal Project must be the student's own, and the role of any outside teacher is to teach, question and give feedback. Nobody should be supplying content that lands in a student's submitted task, and anyone offering to is creating a problem for the student rather than solving one.

Second, the regulator. Abu Dhabi's private schools are licensed and inspected by the Department of Education and Knowledge; the UAE government's portal describes ADEK as supervising the licensing and accreditation of private schools in the emirate. ADEK publishes an inspection record for each school, which is a better guide to a mathematics department's strength than any provider's marketing. Press reporting also describes ADEK professional-ethics rules barring school staff from paid private tutoring of students enrolled at their own school; that should be verified against ADEK's current policy document, but the practical implication is plain enough that your child's own mathematics teacher is the wrong person to pay.

Third, the permit. Private tutoring in the UAE operates under Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, which introduced private tuition work permits. The government portal records that the permit is granted free of charge for two years and that eligible applicants include registered school teachers, government and private-sector employees, unemployed individuals, school students aged fifteen to eighteen and university students. Tutoring without one carries fines and penalties under the applicable laws, with no published fine schedule, so any amount quoted to you is unverified. For the record, IB Gram holds no accreditation or partnership from ADEK, the Ministry of Education, the International Baccalaureate, Cambridge or Pearson, and operates no premises in the UAE.
bullets: Assessed MYP tasks must be the student's own work; a tutor teaches and questions

process.title: Send the four criterion levels and the route
process.description: Four numbers between one and eight, plus confirmation that your child is on the standard route and which MYP year they are in. That is enough to say which criterion is holding the grade down before anybody teaches anything, and it prevents a first session spent on discovery.

process.title: A free first lesson that is a diagnosis
process.description: A short task spanning all four criteria, marked against the descriptors, returned as a written read. It will say which criterion is low, whether the cause is content or technique, and what the realistic unit of change is. If the honest answer is three sessions, that is what you will be told.

process.title: Target the lowest criterion, not the easiest
process.description: The instinct is to work on what feels productive, which is usually the strongest criterion. The grade is held down by the lowest. Sessions are aimed at that one deliberately, with the target written down so progress can be checked against something rather than remembered.

process.title: Re-mark the same style of task
process.description: After four sessions the same kind of task is set again and marked against the same criterion. A level that has moved is evidence. A level that has not is information too, and it usually means the cause was content rather than technique or the other way round.

process.title: Decide about the route with evidence, not pride
process.description: If a route review is the goal, the case is built from secured core content and demonstrated criterion B at the upper bands. The school decides, not a tutor. Where the evidence does not support a review, we will say so, because forcing a student onto extended unprepared helps nobody.

whyPoints.title: Standard taught as a course, not as remediation
whyPoints.description: The standard route has its own syllabus, its own difficulty and a grade ceiling of 7. Teaching it as a lighter version of extended wastes the available levels. Sessions here are about reaching the top descriptor bands on standard material, which is a demanding target in its own right.

whyPoints.title: The syllabuses are published side by side
whyPoints.description: You can see exactly what standard covers, where extended goes further, and what that difference means in a task. That removes the guesswork from a route conversation and stops time being spent on extended content before the standard core is secure.

whyPoints.title: Criterion-level targets, not topic ticks
whyPoints.description: Progress is reported as a criterion level on a re-marked task, because that is what the school's report uses. A list of topics covered tells you what happened in the sessions; a moved criterion level tells you whether it worked.

whyPoints.title: An honest Diploma map
whyPoints.description: Three of the four Diploma mathematics courses follow comfortably from the standard route and one is a genuine stretch. We will name which is which against your child's intended degree rather than flattering a plan that the content does not support.

whyPoints.title: Transfer students diagnosed, not assumed
whyPoints.description: A student arriving from a British, Indian or American system is often placed on standard for want of evidence rather than because of ability. A diagnostic across all four criteria separates a technique gap of weeks from a content gap of a year, which are very different purchases.

whyPoints.title: The delivery model is stated plainly
whyPoints.description: One-to-one lessons online on Gulf Standard Time. IB Gram does not run home visits anywhere in the UAE. For mathematics a shared digital writing surface is better than a notebook on a table, and matching without a driving radius means Al Shamkha gets the same choice as Saadiyat Island.

faqs.question: Is standard mathematics the lower set, or a different course?
faqs.answer: A different route rather than a lower set, although schools often communicate it in a way that sounds like setting. Standard and extended are assessed against the same four criteria, on the same one-to-eight scale, with the same maximum total and the same subject grades up to 7. Extended carries additional depth in algebra and four named topics: quadratics in full, non-right-angled trigonometry, function transformations and conditional probability. Everything else is shared. The practical damage of the lower-set reading is real, because a student who believes the ceiling has dropped stops working towards the top descriptor bands.

faqs.question: Does taking standard mathematics stop my son studying maths in the Diploma?
faqs.answer: No. Every Diploma candidate takes a mathematics course, and three of the four combinations follow comfortably from the standard route. Applications and Interpretation at Standard Level is a direct continuation. Applications and Interpretation at Higher Level is reachable with sustained work and is a serious course, not a soft option. Analysis and Approaches at Standard Level needs a bridging effort concentrated on quadratics and function behaviour. The one that is a genuine stretch is Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level, because it assumes the algebraic fluency the extended route spends two years building.

faqs.question: Can a student actually be awarded a 7 on the standard route?
faqs.answer: Yes, and it is a demanding achievement rather than a technicality. The grade comes from the total of four criterion levels mapped onto the one-to-seven scale, and the criteria are the same on both routes. What a 7 on standard requires is complete security across the standard syllabus plus genuine justification on criterion B and a real evaluation on criterion D. That combination is not reached by drifting. Students miss it far more often by stopping at a described pattern than by lacking extended content, which is why investigation technique is where the effort belongs.

faqs.question: When does the standard and extended split happen, and can a decision be revisited?
faqs.answer: The split normally takes effect at the start of MYP 4, with the decision made at the end of MYP 3 on the basis of criterion levels. Whether it can be revisited depends on the school: larger Abu Dhabi departments with full classes on both routes often review at the end of MYP 4, while smaller ones may not have the timetable to move a student. Ask the head of mathematics directly what the review process is and what evidence it needs. A documented record of rising criterion levels on standard material is the most persuasive thing a family can bring to that conversation.

faqs.question: What topics does the standard route not cover?
faqs.answer: Four areas, broadly. The full quadratic treatment, including manipulation and proof-style reasoning, sits in extended. Non-right-angled trigonometry, meaning the sine and cosine rules, is extended; standard covers right-angled triangles and Pythagoras thoroughly. Function transformations and non-linear function families are extended, while standard works with straight lines, gradient and intercepts in context. Conditional probability is extended; standard handles single and combined events including tree diagrams. Everything in number, ratio, proportion, mensuration, geometry reasoning and statistics is shared, and those shared strands are where most of the available levels sit.

faqs.question: My daughter says standard maths is too easy. Is boredom a reason to move her?
faqs.answer: It is a reason to investigate, not to move immediately. Easy often means the criterion A procedures are comfortable, which is only one of four criteria. Ask what her criterion B levels look like: a student finding the content easy and sitting at a 4 for investigating patterns is not under-challenged, she is under-taught on justification, and extended content will not fix that. If criterion B and D are also strong and she is consistently at the top bands, that is a genuine case for a route review and the evidence to take to the head of mathematics is exactly those levels.

faqs.question: Which Diploma mathematics course follows most naturally from standard?
faqs.answer: Applications and Interpretation, at either level depending on the student. It assumes the statistical and modelling emphasis that the standard route already builds, and at Higher Level it is a substantial course that suits economics, business analytics, psychology and geography routes well. Analysis and Approaches at Standard Level is also a reasonable destination with bridging work on quadratics and functions. The thing to decide first is the intended degree, because that determines which course is required rather than merely comfortable, and that conversation belongs in MYP 4.

faqs.question: Does the on-screen examination differ between the standard and extended routes?
faqs.answer: The paper is pitched at the syllabus the candidate has followed, so a standard-route candidate is not examined on extended content. Entry is a school decision and many Abu Dhabi schools do not enter candidates at all, so confirm it applies before preparing for it. Where it does, the preparation is about format rather than content: reading a scenario on screen, working on paper beside it, and entering responses in an acceptable form. Students who have practised only on paper lose time rather than marks, and the tasks lean towards criteria B and D rather than pure recall.

faqs.question: What does a criterion B investigation look like on the standard route?
faqs.answer: Typically a sequence or a geometric pattern that a student must explore, generalise and then justify. A sample task might give the number of diagonals in polygons with increasing sides, ask for a general rule in terms of the number of sides, and then expect the student to explain why that rule must hold. The top band requires that explanation. A student who finds the correct rule, tests it on three cases and stops has described a pattern, not justified one, and sits in the middle bands however accurate the arithmetic. Standard content is entirely sufficient for the top band.

faqs.question: We moved from a British school into MYP 4 standard. What is actually missing?
faqs.answer: Usually technique rather than content. A student from a Higher-tier British path has met nearly all of the standard syllabus and some extended material, and will find the mathematics familiar. What is new is criterion marking: being required to justify a general rule, to evaluate a model against the situation, and to produce working that reads as reasoning rather than as arithmetic. That is four to six weeks of focused work, not a year of catch-up. Separating the technique gap from a content gap in the first session is the single most useful thing a diagnostic does for a transferring student.

faqs.question: Her report shows 6, 4, 6, 5. Which number should we work on first?
faqs.answer: The 4, and if the criteria are in the usual order that is investigating patterns. The subject grade comes from the total, so the lowest criterion is holding it down and the strongest one has least room to improve. Working on criterion B is slower and less immediately satisfying than more practice questions, which is why families and students both drift towards the stronger criteria. A fortnight of being made to justify general rules, by someone who will not accept a description, is worth more to that profile than a term of extra exercises.

faqs.question: How many sessions does a standard-route student usually need?
faqs.answer: It depends on whether the problem is technique or content, which is why the first lesson is a diagnostic. Criterion C, which is largely notation and logical presentation, usually moves a level in two or three sessions. Criterion D moves in two or three once the evaluation paragraph is taught as a structure. Criterion B is slower, typically a bounded block of six to eight sessions, because justification is a genuine skill rather than a habit. An arithmetic gap carried from primary school needs frequent short practice over a term. Published UAE market rates for a qualified online tutor run AED 150-300 an hour.

faqs.question: Does the school decide the route, or do we?
faqs.answer: The school decides, and it is right that it does, because the decision rests on criterion evidence the department holds. What a family can do is make sure the decision is made on complete information: ask what evidence was used, whether a review happens at the end of MYP 4, and what would need to change for a student to move. In some Abu Dhabi schools, particularly newer ones with small departments, the decision is also constrained by timetabling rather than by judgement, and it is worth asking whether that is the real factor before building a case.

faqs.question: Will a UAE university care which MYP mathematics route my child took?
faqs.answer: Not directly. Universities look at the Diploma, so what matters is which Diploma mathematics course your child takes and what grade they achieve in it. The MYP route matters only because it shapes which Diploma course is realistic. Note also that Ministry of Education equivalency is a separate process with its own published requirements by curriculum, and no IB points threshold for equivalency should be relied upon unless you have read it on an official Ministry source. Equivalency is not something a tutoring provider performs or guarantees; it is handled through the official channel.

faqs.question: Is it worth paying for maths support if she is coping on the standard route?
faqs.answer: Only if there is a specific target. Coping at a 5 with no plan to reach a 6 is not a reason to spend money. Two situations do justify it. The first is an uneven profile where one criterion is dragging the grade down and a bounded block would lift it, which is a concrete and finite job. The second is a Diploma plan that needs Analysis and Approaches, in which case the bridging work is better started in MYP 5 than in DP1. Absent either, the honest advice is to keep the money and check the next report.

faqs.question: What does a session do that extra homework does not?
faqs.answer: Three things homework cannot. It refuses to accept a described pattern as a justification, which is the only reliable way to move criterion B. It marks the working rather than the answer, so a solution with a correct result and a broken line of reasoning is caught rather than ticked. And it diagnoses: a tutor watching a student attempt a problem sees whether the obstacle is the method, the arithmetic underneath it, or the reading of the question. Extra exercises on a topic the student can already do will fill an evening and leave the criterion levels exactly where they were.

abu-dhabi/ib-myp-standard-mathematics-tu.closingHeading: Send the levels, and we will tell you which one is holding the grade
abu-dhabi/ib-myp-standard-mathematics-tu.closingBody: If you are looking for an IB MYP standard mathematics tutor in Abu Dhabi, start by sending the four criterion levels from the last report and the MYP year. The first lesson is free and ends in a written read: which criterion is low, whether the cause is content or technique, and what the realistic unit of change is. intro.heading: Why MYP tutoring looks nothing like exam coaching
paragraphs: Most parents arrive at an IB MYP tutor in Abu Dhabi holding a report card they cannot read. There are no percentages on it. Instead there are four letters per subject, each carrying a number between 0 and 8, and a single figure between 1 and 7 that the school says is the grade. Nothing on the page says which topic went wrong, and the comment underneath tends to describe effort rather than attainment. The instinct is to ask for more practice. The useful first step is to work out which of the four criteria is actually dragging the grade down, because they are not fixed by the same thing and three of them are rarely fixed by practice at all.

The Middle Years Programme is assessed against published criteria rather than against a syllabus of examinable content. Each subject has four of them, each scored from 0 to 8 by best fit against descriptors, and a teacher marks each task against only the criteria that task was designed to assess. That is why one child can hold a 7 in knowing and understanding and a 3 in investigating, and why the resulting grade of 5 tells you almost nothing on its own. A tutor who talks about percentages, revision guides and past papers in MYP 3 has not understood what the school is measuring.

This page is built around what can be evidenced. Not a promise about a grade, which nobody can honestly make, but the record a term of tutoring should leave behind: the marked tasks and what each one shows, a log of lost levels sorted by criterion, dated drafts for any longer piece of work, and session notes naming what was addressed. Those four artefacts are what let a parent judge whether tutoring is working while there is still a term left to change course. Grade movement in the MYP is lumpy and slow, because a criterion level moves only when a new task assessing that criterion comes round.

Abu Dhabi adds its own specifics. ADEK licenses and inspects the emirate's private schools and publishes its own ratings, so the school's internal assessment calendar is set against ADEK requirements rather than any external board timetable. Several schools here run the MYP and then offer both the Diploma and IGCSE at the end of MYP 5, which turns Year 11 into a decision year as well as an assessment one. Federal rules also require Arabic, Islamic Education and social studies alongside the licensed curriculum, so an MYP student in Khalifa City or on Al Reem Island carries more subjects than the eight MYP groups suggest.

On delivery, so there is no ambiguity before you read further: IB Gram does not offer home visits in Abu Dhabi, and in-home tutoring is a service we run only in India. MYP sessions for Abu Dhabi families are one-to-one over live video. That is also what makes criterion-level matching possible, because the tutor who has actually taught MYP Sciences criterion C to a Year 9 cohort is matched to your child regardless of whether they live within driving distance of Al Raha.

abu-dhabi/ib-myp-tutor.programmesIntro: The Middle Years Programme sits between two others, and each handover changes how progress is measured. Knowing which programme your child is in, and what comes next at your particular Abu Dhabi school, decides what a tutor should be working on this term.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Eight subject groups, each assessed against four published criteria scored 0-8 by best-fit judgement against descriptors. Tasks carry task-specific clarifications written by the teacher. The final year adds the Personal Project, supervised in school, and some schools enter students for on-screen eAssessment or ePortfolios.
programmes.countryNote: In Abu Dhabi the MYP years are where families start comparing routes, because several schools here offer both the Diploma and IGCSE after MYP 5. The practical effect is that MYP 4 and MYP 5 tutoring has two jobs at once: raising criterion levels now, and generating enough evidence to make the Year 11 route decision on something better than a hunch.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: Inquiry-led and without external examination, judged through portfolios, teacher observation and whatever standardised measures the school runs. The final year carries the Exhibition. Students arrive in MYP 1 strong on inquiry habits and often light on written structure under time pressure.
programmes.countryNote: The MYP 1 intake in Abu Dhabi mixes PYP graduates with arrivals from British, Indian and American systems in the same class. Tutors see the gap most clearly in criterion-referenced writing: the PYP child can investigate and the British-system child can structure, and each is missing what the other has.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects with three at Higher Level, plus Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and Creativity, Activity, Service. Assessed by external written papers with an internally marked, externally moderated component in each subject. Grades are 1-7 per subject against published criteria and boundaries.
programmes.countryNote: The MYP to Diploma step is where Abu Dhabi families most often ask for help, and the honest answer depends on criterion-level patterns rather than on the overall grade. A student holding consistent 6s and 7s in knowing and understanding but 3s in investigating will find Higher Level sciences harder than their report card suggests.

programmes.name: The IGCSE alternative after MYP 5
programmes.description: Several Abu Dhabi schools run Cambridge or Pearson Edexcel IGCSE courses in Years 10 and 11 instead of, or alongside, MYP 4 and 5. Assessment switches to externally examined papers with syllabus codes and tiering decisions, which is a different kind of preparation entirely.
programmes.countryNote: If your child's Abu Dhabi school moves students from MYP 3 into IGCSE in Year 10, the tutoring brief changes in the summer term of MYP 3. Criterion descriptors stop mattering and syllabus content starts, and a tutor who has only taught the MYP will keep coaching the wrong thing for a term.

abu-dhabi/ib-myp-tutor.subjectsIntro: Each MYP subject group has its own four criteria, and the criterion that costs your child levels is usually the same one across several subjects. The notes below name what each group assesses and where levels most often sit lowest for Abu Dhabi students.

subjects.name: Language and Literature
subjects.description: Criteria cover analysing, organising, producing text and using language. Levels drop most in analysing, where students summarise a text instead of commenting on how it works, and in using language, where register and control are judged rather than vocabulary breadth.

subjects.name: Language Acquisition
subjects.description: Listening, reading, speaking and writing, each with its own criterion, assessed in phases rather than year groups. The commonest loss is in speaking, because it is the least practised at home, and in writing, where students are marked on task type and register as much as on accuracy.

subjects.name: Individuals and Societies
subjects.description: Knowing and understanding, investigating, communicating and thinking critically. Investigating carries a research-process requirement that most students underestimate, and thinking critically is where a well-written essay with no counter-argument stalls at a 4 or 5.

subjects.name: Sciences
subjects.description: Knowing and understanding, inquiring and designing, processing and evaluating, and reflecting on the impacts of science. The investigation criteria are where levels are won and lost; the fourth criterion is the single most neglected in the programme because it is rarely practised outside a formal task.

subjects.name: Mathematics
subjects.description: Knowing and understanding, investigating patterns, communicating, and applying mathematics in real-life contexts. Strong arithmetic students routinely sit low on investigating patterns, which requires generalising and justifying rather than calculating, and on communicating, which marks presentation of reasoning.

subjects.name: Design
subjects.description: Inquiring and analysing, developing ideas, creating the solution and evaluating. Almost all lost levels come from documentation rather than from the artefact: a working product with a design folder that does not evidence the criteria will score below a modest product that does.

subjects.name: Arts
subjects.description: Investigating and knowing, developing skills, thinking creatively and responding. Students who perform or draw well often lose levels on the process journal, where the thinking behind the work has to be visible rather than simply good.

subjects.name: Physical and Health Education
subjects.description: Knowing and understanding, planning for performance, applying and performing, and reflecting on performance. The written criteria surprise families: a capable athlete can finish a unit on a 4 because the planning and reflection components were treated as optional.

subjects.name: Arabic as a first and additional language
subjects.description: Arabic runs both as an MYP language subject and as a federally required subject in UAE private schools, and the two briefs are different. Say which stream your child is in, because the expectations, the language of instruction and the material are not the same.

subjects.name: Interdisciplinary units
subjects.description: Assessed against their own criteria, usually evaluating, synthesising and reflecting, and reported separately in many schools. Students who are strong in each contributing subject still lose levels here, because the task rewards connecting two disciplines rather than performing in either.

regions.name: Yas Island
regions.note: Younger MYP cohorts, with MYP 1 and MYP 2 requests more common here than elsewhere. The work is mostly writing structure and the transition out of PYP-style inquiry into criterion-marked tasks with deadlines.

sections.heading: What an MYP report card actually says, and what it does not
paragraphs: An MYP report card reports four criterion levels per subject, each between 0 and 8, and a converted grade between 1 and 7. It does not report a percentage, a rank, or a topic list, and it is not designed to. Each criterion is a different competence, judged by best fit against published descriptors, and a teacher marks any given task against only the criteria that task was built to assess. That is why your child's levels in one subject can look inconsistent: they were awarded on different tasks, at different times, for different things.

The letters are not interchangeable between subject groups. Criterion A in Sciences is knowing and understanding; criterion A in Design is inquiring and analysing; criterion A in Language Acquisition is listening. Parents comparing two subjects on their child's report are frequently comparing unlike things and concluding that the child is inconsistent when the pattern is actually clear. Read down the column of what each criterion measures rather than across the row of letters.

What the report does tell you, read properly, is where the hours should go. A child sitting at 6 or 7 on knowing and understanding across several subjects has the content. If the same child sits at 3 or 4 on the investigating and communicating criteria, the problem is process and presentation of reasoning, which no amount of revision will touch. That diagnosis takes ten minutes with the report in front of you, and it is the single most useful thing a first session with an MYP tutor can produce.

sections.heading: From four criterion levels to one grade, and what a single level is worth
paragraphs: The conversion is mechanical and worth understanding, because it explains why a grade can sit still while real progress is happening underneath it. The four criterion levels are summed, giving a total out of 32, and that total is converted to a grade from 1 to 7 using the boundaries published in each subject guide. Schools apply the same published boundaries, so the arithmetic is not a matter of opinion, but the exact ranges belong to the guide rather than to a tutoring page. Ask your child's MYP coordinator for the conversion table the school uses; they will have it and will share it.

Two consequences follow. The first is that a grade of 5 can hide very different profiles. A child with four balanced levels around 5 and a child holding two 7s and two 3s can land on the same grade and need completely different work. The second is that moving one criterion by two levels can move the final grade, while moving all four by half a level may not move it at all. That is why a tutor should name a target criterion rather than a target grade: the criterion is the thing the work can actually shift.

It also explains the timing problem that frustrates parents most. A criterion level only changes when a new task assessing that criterion is marked, and in some subjects that happens twice a term. Tutoring started in week three may produce no visible report change until the following term, even where the underlying work is sound. This is why the record matters more than the grade in the short run, and why anyone promising a grade movement inside a few weeks is describing something the assessment calendar does not permit.

sections.heading: Reading a marked MYP task without being a subject teacher
paragraphs: Every formal MYP task comes with task-specific clarifications: the teacher's rewriting of the generic descriptors into the language of that particular piece of work. Those clarifications are the marking instrument, and most families never read them. When a marked task comes back, put the clarifications beside the awarded level and find the sentence in the descriptor band above the one your child received. The gap between those two sentences is the entire tutoring brief for that criterion, stated in the school's own words.

Levels are awarded by best fit, not by adding up ticks. A piece of work that does three things in the 7-8 band and one thing in the 3-4 band will usually land in the middle, which feels unfair to a student who did some excellent work. The practical lesson is that consistency across a descriptor beats brilliance in part of it, and that is a coachable habit rather than a talent. Students who learn to check their work against each strand of the descriptor before submitting it gain a level or two without learning any new content.

What a parent can judge without subject knowledge is whether the feedback is diagnostic. A comment reading more detail needed is not usable. A comment that says the method section does not explain why the variable was controlled, which is what the band above requires, is usable, and a tutor's job in the first fortnight is to turn the first kind into the second. If your child's tasks come back with marks and no descriptor references, that is worth raising with the school before paying anyone.

sections.heading: Eight weeks of MYP tutoring, week by week
paragraphs: A term of tutoring should be auditable, and the simplest way to make it auditable is to agree in advance what exists at the end of each fortnight. The sequence below is what a competent MYP brief looks like, and it is deliberately front-loaded with diagnosis, because starting the teaching before the diagnosis is how families end up paying for the wrong subject for a term.

The first two weeks produce the diagnosis and the baseline. The tutor reads the report card, the most recent two marked tasks and their clarifications, then watches your child attempt one task unaided to see where the work actually stops. By the end of week two there should be a named target criterion, a short written statement of what the band above requires, and a log of lost levels sorted by cause. Weeks three to six are the working weeks: a short task each week assessing the target criterion, marked against the published descriptors, with the strands checked before submission rather than after.

Weeks seven and eight are the review. By then at least one school-marked task assessing the target criterion should have come back, and there are three honest outcomes. The level has moved, in which case the next criterion gets named. The level has not moved but the tutor's own marked tasks show the strand improving, in which case continue through the next school task. Or nothing has moved anywhere, in which case the match or the diagnosis is wrong, and the right response is to change one of them rather than to buy more hours.

sections.heading: Where MYP levels actually drop, criterion by criterion
paragraphs: Across subject groups, the losses concentrate in the same two places. The first is the investigation and inquiry criteria: inquiring and designing in Sciences, investigating in Individuals and Societies, investigating patterns in Mathematics, inquiring and analysing in Design. These reward a documented process, and students who think fast and write little are punished by them regardless of how strong their answers are. The fix is a process habit rather than content teaching, which is why it is slow at first and then holds permanently.

The second is the final criterion in most groups, the one that asks for reflection, evaluation or application to real contexts. Reflecting on the impacts of science, applying mathematics in real-life contexts, evaluating in Design, responding in Arts. These are the least rehearsed strands in the programme because they rarely appear in homework, and they are worth up to a quarter of the total on their own. A student who has never been taught what a strong reflection looks like will produce a description of what they did, which sits at the bottom of the band.

Communicating sits between the two as the most underestimated criterion of all. In Mathematics it marks whether reasoning is presented so that a reader can follow it, which is a different skill from getting the answer right, and bright students who work in their heads lose levels here for years without anyone naming it. A tutor working on communicating is not teaching content at all; they are making a student show their working in a form that satisfies a descriptor, and it is often the fastest single level available.
